entry.title: Manyat Thinking: Weight Variance — Block the Risk, Not Every Truck
entry.content:
Manyat Thinking: Weight Variance — Block the Risk, Not Every Truck

A design perspective on tolerance-based discrepancy handling

across SAP EWM, TM, and Situation Handling

Business First. SAP Second.

Introduction

In warehouse and transportation operations, weight discrepancy is often treated as a simple control problem. The standard reaction can easily become:

Planned Weight ≠ Actual Weight → Block the Process

At first glance, this looks safe. But what happens when every discrepancy immediately stops the truck? The vehicle waits. The yard starts filling. Loading and dispatch operations slow down. And eventually, a control designed to protect the business can become an operational bottleneck.

Should every weight discrepancy block execution, or should the system first understand the level of risk?

A discrepancy should first be classified, not automatically blocked.

1.  The Ground Reality

Weight differences can appear at different points in the physical process: planned weight, loading weight, weighbridge weight, transportation execution data, receiving weight.

A difference can have several possible causes: scale calibration, moisture or natural weight loss, packaging differences, measurement variation, loading conditions, or an actual unexplained quantity difference.

So the system should not immediately treat every difference as the same type of exception.

What does this discrepancy actually mean for the business?

2.  The Traditional Approach

A simple control can look like this:

Technically, this looks controlled. Operationally, however, it can create another problem. If investigation takes time, the truck remains at the origin. Now imagine this happening across multiple vehicles:

The system has protected one control point but potentially damaged the overall warehouse flow.

So I would not start with "How can SAP block this truck?" I would start with:

What level of risk does this discrepancy represent?

3.  The Manyat Approach: Risk Classification

The architecture should introduce one additional decision layer.

This changes the architecture completely. The system is no longer saying Difference = Block. Instead:

Difference = Evaluate Risk

4.  But What If Blocking Costs More Than the Risk?

Suppose goods value is ₹5,000, but stopping the truck creates a delay penalty of ₹10,000:

"Control ka cost risk se bada to nahi ho gaya?"

In professional terms: is the cost of the control greater than the business risk we are trying to control? This does not mean cost should always override risk — a critical security or compliance risk may still require a hard block regardless of delay cost. The point is to make the decision consciously.

5.  Decision Flow

 The real control point is the decision.

6.  Three Business Decisions

Situation

Risk

Delay Cost

Decision

Seal broken

High

₹10,000

Hard Block

Weight variance under review

₹10,000

Continue + Targeted Verification

7.  Example: +120 KG Difference

Plant A shipment: Planned Gross Weight = 10,000 KG, Tolerance = 50 KG, Actual Weight = 10,120 KG.

Tolerance breach does not automatically have to mean process block. It can mean: Evaluate the risk.

8.  Soft Attention Instead of Immediate Blocking

The truck does not automatically become the victim of the system's uncertainty.

9.  But If We Don't Block, How Do We Manage the Risk?

Continue ≠ Ignore. If a variance requires verification, the business still needs a control mechanism.

10.  Who Should Receive the Alert?

11.  Situation Handling: Attention, Not Enforcement

Situation Handling can bring the right business situation to the attention of the right person.

12.  Destination Verification

13.  Not Every Difference Means Theft

The business process should determine what the difference means.

14.  Soft Attention vs Hard Block

Situation

Response

Small / explainable variance

Continue + Record

Verification-required variance

Soft Situation + Targeted Verification

Significant unexplained variance

Escalation / Investigation

Critical security or compliance risk

Hard Block

Confirmed inventory discrepancy

Appropriate Inventory / Process Action

15.  Why This Architecture Is Different

16.  EWM, TM and Yard Should Not Be Designed in Isolation

17.  The Real Control Point Is Not the Truck

18.  Targeted Verification

19.  This Is Not "Ignore the Exception"

20.  SAP Configuration Comes After the Business Decision

21.  The Manyat Thinking Principle

Conclusion

A weight discrepancy is an important operational signal. But a signal should not automatically become a system lock.

What level of risk does this discrepancy represent, and what is the least disruptive control that still protects the business?

The architecture therefore becomes: Detect → Classify → Decide → Act → Validate Outcome.

Do not block every discrepancy. Block the risk that truly requires blocking.

MANYAT THINKING

Business First. SAP Second.

entry.title: Pick-by-Voice in EWM: The Problem Wasn’t the Voice - It Was What We Made It Say
entry.content:
Pick-by-Voice in EWM: The Problem Wasn’t the Voice - It Was What We Made It Say

Introduction

Pick-by-Voice in SAP EWM is one of those technologies that looks very simple when you see it working for the first time. The operator wears a headset, SAP EWM guides the picking process, the operator responds using voice commands, and the system moves to the next step. From a technical perspective, once the device, voice solution, RF transaction and SAP configuration are connected, it can feel like the difficult part is already behind you.

My experience was different.

On my first Pick-by-Voice project, the solution was technically working as expected. The device was connected, the RF transaction was functioning, the prompts were being played and the operators were able to respond. But shortly after go-live, I learned that a solution being technically correct does not necessarily mean that it is comfortable or efficient for the person using it.

One of the experienced pickers told me something very simple: “The headset is talking too much.”

That sentence changed the way I looked at Pick-by-Voice. The problem was not that the system could not speak. The problem was that we had made it say too much.

The Day I Realized the Problem Wasn’t the Voice

My first reaction was to think about the speech rate. If the system was speaking too much, perhaps we could make it speak faster. So, I discussed it with the voice vendor and we tried increasing the speech rate.

It sounded like a logical solution. It wasn't.

As the speech became faster, the voice interaction became less forgiving and the overall experience was not necessarily better. That was when I decided to stop looking at the problem from the system's perspective and actually experience it from the operator's perspective.

I put on the headset and went through the picking process myself.

The system was reading the source bin, the handling unit, the product, the quantity and the unit of measure. Technically, all of that information was correct. But when you are standing in a warehouse and trying to pick efficiently, hearing a long handling unit number read out completely is a very different experience.

The HU number was already available on the label in front of the operator. We did not necessarily need the system to speak every digit of a long number. The voice dialogue was technically complete, but operationally it was too verbose.

That led us to a much simpler question: Does the operator really need to hear this?

Instead of trying to make the voice talk faster, we started looking at what the voice actually needed to say.

In that project, we shortened the information being spoken, including using only the relevant part of the HU identification, and removed information that was not necessary for the operator at that point in the process. We also looked at the order in which information was presented.

Interestingly, this is not just a project-specific idea. SAP's standard Pick-by-Voice logic itself has HU validation designed to avoid making the operator speak the complete HU number. EWM can determine the minimum number of digits from the end of the HU number required to identify it uniquely within the storage bin.

The lesson for me was straightforward: the best voice optimization is not always speaking faster. Sometimes it is simply saying less.

That experience also made me look more closely at what is happening inside SAP EWM when a voice dialogue is running.

Where the Voice Conversation Actually Happens

SAP Pick-by-Voice is built around the EWM RF framework and the RF picking transaction, together with the ITS template generator for mobile devices with speech input. SAP EWM uses SAPGUI dynpros whose fields contain speech-related properties, and the system generates HTML templates containing speech-specific tags that are interpreted by the browser on the voice device.

The important point is that SAP EWM remains responsible for the warehouse process and RF dialogue, while the voice platform and device layer provide the speech interaction and recognition required by the solution. The exact architecture can vary depending on the voice solution being used.

This distinction matters when troubleshooting a voice issue.

When an operator says, “The voice is too slow,” “The system is asking for too much information,” or “It doesn't understand me,” the answer may not be to change something in the voice engine.

Sometimes the real issue is the SAP dialogue we designed.

The SAP EWM Controls Behind the Dialogue

SAP EWM provides several speech-related properties that influence how a field participates in the Pick-by-Voice dialogue. Among the key properties are PromptText, HelpText, FilledText, Grammar and GrammarLnk.

PromptText defines the text used to prompt the operator for input. HelpText can be spoken when the input is not recognized, while FilledText can be used after speech input has been successfully detected. Grammar defines the grammar used to recognize speech input, while GrammarLnk allows the grammar to be loaded externally. SAP documentation also describes attributes such as TimeOut and NextField, which can influence the speech dialogue flow.

SAP's Pick-by-Voice documentation states that a screen can contain up to ten prompts, grammars and help texts.

These properties give you considerable control over the conversation, but I don't think they should be treated simply as technical fields to be populated.

They determine what the warehouse operator hears and what the system expects the operator to say.

That makes them part of the warehouse user experience.

Using the BAdI to Change What the Operator Hears

One of the useful enhancement points for this is the Modify Screen Field Voice Properties BAdI.

SAP provides this BAdI under the EWM Mobile Data Entry area, and it can be used to change the voice properties of the screen and its fields before the screen is presented to the user. SAP introduced this BAdI specifically as part of the Pick-by-Voice functionality.

This is important because the voice dialogue does not always have to be completely static.

The voice properties can be influenced based on the actual process and data being handled. This gives you the flexibility to make the dialogue more relevant instead of forcing every operator through exactly the same amount of spoken information.

Going back to my HU example, if EWM knows the complete HU number, that does not automatically mean the operator needs to hear the complete number.

The technical question is:

What value does the field contain?

The business question is:

What does the operator actually need to hear?

Those are two different questions.

And that distinction is where a lot of the practical optimization happens.

Grammar Matters as Much as the Prompt

There is another side to the conversation that is easy to overlook: what the system expects the operator to say.

A good voice dialogue is not only about creating clear prompts. The grammar also needs to be designed carefully. If the expected vocabulary is unnecessarily broad or the grammar is complicated, the voice interaction can become harder to recognize and troubleshoot.

For example, a quantity field normally does not need a large vocabulary. The expected response is generally a number, together with whatever confirmation or help options the process requires.

Keeping the expected grammar focused makes the interaction more predictable.

Bin verification is another good example.

SAP's standard Pick-by-Voice functionality does not necessarily require the operator to repeat a complete storage bin. The storage bin can be split into components such as storage type, aisle, stack and level, with the appropriate validation used for each part. SAP also documents a mechanism where only the difference between the previous and current storage bin needs to be spoken when the relevant information remains unchanged.

The same principle applies to HU validation. SAP documents a specific PbV validation logic that can determine how many digits from the end of an HU number are required to uniquely identify it in the storage bin. For example, instead of speaking a complete HU number, the operator may only need to speak the required trailing digits.

This is exactly the kind of detail that demonstrates why voice dialogue should be designed together with the warehouse process.

The goal is not to make the system say everything it knows.

The goal is to make the operator say and hear only what is necessary.

Commands Are Part of the Conversation Too

Pick-by-Voice is not only about reading fields and accepting values. Commands are also part of the interaction.

SAP's Pick-by-Voice transaction supports commands that allow the operator to control the dialogue. The operator can enter command mode using the integrated Command keyword, and the Okay command corresponds to the Enter pushbutton. SAP also documents the use of voice-related properties and command buttons as part of the RF dialogue.

These details may sound small, but they become important when designing a voice process that feels natural.

The operator should not have to remember an unnecessarily complicated set of commands just to move through a standard picking flow.

Commands should support the process rather than become another process the operator has to learn.

What I Would Do Differently Today

If I were starting another Pick-by-Voice implementation today, I would involve the warehouse operators much earlier in the design of the dialogue.

Not just during UAT. Not just after the configuration is finished.

I would actually put the headset on during design and walk through the real picking process.

I would ask simple questions. What information do you need to hear? What information is already visible on the label? Which numbers are difficult to understand when spoken? Which prompts feel repetitive? Which responses are natural for the operator and which ones feel like something designed by a system rather than a person?

I would also test the dialogue at realistic warehouse speed.

A prompt that sounds perfectly reasonable when someone is sitting in a meeting room can feel completely different when the operator is moving through a warehouse, handling a pallet or carton and trying to maintain a picking rhythm.

That is probably the biggest lesson I took from my first project. Pick-by-Voice should be designed with the operator's ears in mind, not only the developer's screen.

Conclusion

Getting Pick-by-Voice technically connected to SAP EWM is an important part of the implementation, but it is not the end of the work.

The real challenge starts when you ask whether the conversation makes sense to the person wearing the headset.

My first instinct was to make the voice speak faster. The better solution was to make the system speak less. That experience changed how I look at voice implementations in EWM.

A prompt can be technically correct and still be a poor warehouse prompt. A grammar can be valid and still be unnecessarily complicated. A piece of information can be available in EWM and still not need to be spoken.

For me, the most important principle is simple:

Don't ask how much information the system can say. Ask how much information the operator actually needs to hear.

Pick-by-Voice works best when the technology stays in the background, and the dialogue feels natural to the person doing the work.

That is where the real optimization begins.

entry.title: What Drives It All: The Compliance Data Foundation in SAP S/4HANA for Product Compliance
entry.content:
This post builds on and complements a previous article in which we introduced the three core capabilities of SAP S/4HANA for Product Compliance. If you haven't read the blog post “Product Compliance in SAP S/4HANA: How Three Integrated Capabilities Enable Safe Global Operations” yet, you can find it here: Product Compliance in SAP S/4HANA: How Three Integrated Capabilities Enable Safe Global Operations

In this post, we go one level deeper and take a closer look at what drives all three capabilities: the Compliance Data Foundation.

This foundation is your single source of truth for regulatory execution. At its core: Compliance Requirements, Purposes, and Content that work together across three key capabilities: Product Marketability & Component Compliance, Dangerous Goods Management and Compliance Document Management.

The already mentioned Compliance Requirements are the semantic anchor, and deliverable building blocks that capture the obligations from a regulation, part of a regulation, or a stakeholder requirement. Think of examples like "Labeling according to GHS," or "Dangerous Goods Classification according to ADN or IATA." 

Compliance Requirements are assigned to a product through Compliance Purposes which are self-configurable bundles that group the relevant compliance requirements based on a specific obligation a company needs to fulfill. A Compliance Purpose can be created for a country, a region, a customer group, a product type, or a business process. They are highly flexible and can be defined however your use case demands.

And here is what makes the Compliance Data Foundation so powerful:
When regulations change, the update flows through the foundation straight into execution, no manual intervention across multiple places.

The result? Consistent, audit-ready compliance logic that scales with your business and keeps pace with an ever-evolving regulatory landscape.

To learn more about the Compliance Data Foundation, take a look at the new accompanying video: In brief: SAP Product Compliance - Compliance Data Foundation

entry.title: Your Supply Chain Needs to Think for Itself. Agentic AI Makes That Possible
entry.content:
Picture this. It's a Tuesday morning. Diesel prices have just doubled. A key shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz is blocked. Your container vessel is rerouted around Africa, adding 10 days to delivery. And somewhere in your supplier network, a compliance flag has just tripped on a tier-two vendor you hadn't thought about since last quarter.

In the old world, you'd spend the morning on the phone. You'd pull in the planning team, the procurement lead, the logistics manager. You'd run scenarios manually. By the time you had a decision, the situation had already moved on.

What if none of that required a single phone call?

That's not a hypothetical. It's the promise (and increasingly, the reality) of agentic AI in supply chain management. And right now, it couldn't be more relevant. CNN reported this month that U.S. companies are experiencing supply chain instability deeper than anything they faced during COVID-19. Diesel prices have doubled since March. Global container shipping schedule reliability has fallen to just 29% on time, which is close to pandemic-era lows, according to analyst Xeneta. The disruptions are not easing. If anything, they're converging.

The question isn't whether your supply chain needs to respond faster. It's whether it still needs a human to start the process.

From Alert to Action

For the past few years, AI in supply chain has meant better visibility. Smarter dashboards. Earlier warnings. Systems that tell your planners something is wrong and let them decide what to do about it.

Agentic AI is different. These are systems that don't just surface a risk, they act on it. They monitor supplier networks, assess exposure, trigger corrective workflows, reroute inventory, pause non-compliant purchases, and coordinate cross-functional responses, all within governance parameters your business defines.

The shift sounds subtle. It isn't. Moving from "here's a problem" to "here's what I've already done about it" is the difference between a supply chain that reacts and one that recovers before you even knew there was an issue.

What It Looks Like in Practice

C.H. Robinson, one of the world's largest logistics companies, deployed a fleet of more than 30 AI agents that processed over three million freight shipment tasks in 2025. Not recommendations. Tasks. Executed autonomously.

In a recent Autonomous Supply Chain article, SAP’s Hagen Heubach spotlighted that agentic AI is improving procurement workflow efficiency by 20 to 30%, reducing inventory by 20 to 30%, and cutting logistics costs by 5 to 20% in early deployments. In manufacturing settings, it has reduced scrap by 55% and cut nonperfect batches by 80%.

And on the resilience side: the World Economic Forum, drawing on a survey of organizations advancing toward autonomous supply chain capabilities, found they expect to cut disruption response times by 62% — reducing average response from 11 days to just four.

That's not an incremental improvement. That's a different operating model.

The Numbers Are Starting to Stack Up

McKinsey estimates agentic AI can reduce cost of goods sold by 4 to 7% and improve supply chain productivity by 20 to 50%. BCG projects working capital reductions of up to 30% and EBITDA improvements of 2 to 4 percentage points for some organizations.

We are not there yet. But the trajectory is clear, and the gap between companies building toward it and those waiting to see how it plays out is widening every quarter.

How does your organization compare?

The Catch: Governance Has to Keep Pace

Here is where the honest conversation begins. Agentic AI can act faster than any human team. But speed without guardrails is not a competitive advantage, it's a liability.

A 2026 Relex survey found that while 67% of supply chain leaders are more confident in AI than a year ago, only 10% say they trust AI for making critical decisions without human review. That gap tells you something important: the technology is ahead of the governance frameworks most companies have in place.

Getting the most out of agentic AI means investing not just in the technology, but in the data foundations, integration architecture, and oversight structures that let it operate safely at speed. The companies that will win are not the ones that simply deploy agents — they're the ones that design the right boundaries for those agents to work within.

The era of the reactive supply chain is ending. The era of the autonomous supply chain is beginning. Not because the technology is perfect, but because the disruption environment we are operating in no longer has the patience for slow, sequential human decision-making.

The question for every supply chain leader right now is not whether agentic AI belongs in your operating model. It's whether your data, your governance, and your organization are ready to let it run.

entry.title: Stop Overengineering Document Links Unlocking GOS as the Situation Handling Speed Layer
entry.content:
Stop Overengineering Document Links: Unlocking GOS as the Situation Handling Speed Layer

Manyat Thinking | Business First. SAP Second.

The Real Business Problem

A warehouse exception can look very simple on the ground. An operator may find a weight variance, a broken seal, a damaged pallet, or a product condition that requires visual evidence.

The natural reaction is often to start thinking about the SAP object, notification, document, repository, or integration that should be used.

But the better starting point is the business situation itself.

What does the business actually need at that moment?

Consider a simple broken-seal scenario. An operator receives a pallet and discovers that its seal is broken. The operator takes a photograph as evidence.

At this point, several different requirements exist.

The photograph is evidence. Someone needs to know that the exception requires attention. A physical action may follow, which is execution. Later, the business may need to understand what actually happened, which is history.

These requirements are connected, but they are not the same requirement.

That distinction is where the architecture should begin.

What Is Manyat Thinking?

Manyat Thinking is my personal business-first way of designing SAP solutions.

It starts with the physical situation, asks WHY, identifies the actual business requirement, and only then maps that requirement to the appropriate SAP capability and technical implementation.

The thinking flow is:

Ground Reality → Exception → WHY → Root Cause → Business Requirement → Business Decision → SAP Capability → Technical Implementation → Practical Application

This is not intended to replace standard SAP solution architecture or introduce a new SAP methodology.

It is simply a practical way of approaching an SAP problem from the business side first.

The core question is:

What does the business actually need, and which SAP capability naturally owns that requirement?

A Worked Example: Broken Seal

The operator has found a broken seal.

The first requirement is evidence. The photograph needs to remain associated with the relevant business context. Where supported by the relevant business object/application, GOS or the applicable attachment capability can provide that function.

The second requirement is attention. The photograph itself does not determine who needs to act. Situation Handling has a different responsibility: bringing the relevant business situation to the attention of the responsible user.

The third requirement is action. Suppose the responsible user decides that the affected HU must be moved to a clarification or quarantine area. The physical warehouse movement belongs to the existing EWM execution process.

The fourth requirement is history. After the warehouse action is completed, the business may need to know what happened, when it happened, and what warehouse execution was confirmed.

So the architecture becomes:

Evidence → GOS / Attachment Attention → Situation Handling Warehouse Action → EWM Execution Warehouse Execution History → EWM Warehouse Task History

This is the important architectural separation.

The problem is not really a single "notification/document" problem. It is several business requirements that happen to originate from the same physical exception.

Business Requirement → SAP Capability

Once the requirements are separated, the mapping becomes much clearer.

Business Requirement SAP Capability Technical Reference

Store visual evidenceGOS / AttachmentGOS capability where supported by the relevant business object/application
Bring exception to responsible userSituation HandlingManage Situation Types — F2947
Execute warehouse actionExisting EWM process / Warehouse TaskDepends on process design
Record confirmed warehouse executionEWM Warehouse Task History/SCWM/ORDIM_C
Structured enterprise document managementDMSWhen a genuine DMS requirement exists

This table is not intended to replace the architecture. It makes the responsibility of each capability visible.

The important relationship is:

Business Requirement → SAP Capability → Technical Implementation

That is the point where business thinking connects with SAP implementation.

One Business Situation, Different SAP Responsibilities

A common design mistake is to make one technical mechanism responsible for everything simply because all the information came from the same exception.

That is not necessary.

GOS / Attachment can maintain the supporting evidence where the relevant business object supports it. Situation Handling can bring the business situation to the responsible user. EWM can execute the physical warehouse movement through its existing process. EWM execution history can provide the record of confirmed warehouse execution.

The capabilities work together, but they do not need to become one combined technical layer.

This is also why a notification should not automatically become an evidence repository, and an evidence repository should not automatically become the warehouse execution mechanism.

Direct Access: The Speed Layer

A user receiving a situation should not have to search through unrelated repositories simply to understand the exception.

The practical path should be as direct as the scenario allows:

Situation → Relevant Business Context → Evidence → Decision

Situation Handling provides the attention. GOS provides the evidence where supported by the relevant business object/application. EWM provides the physical execution.

The exact navigation or action available to the user depends on the Situation Handling scenario, business object, application and configuration.

In this article, I use "speed layer" as a design term for the shortest practical path from a business situation to its supporting evidence. It is not an SAP product name or a standard SAP architectural layer.

The principle is simple:

Do not create another technical layer merely to make information reachable when the existing business context can already provide the required path.

When the Business Says: "We Need History"

One of the easiest ways to overengineer an architecture is to say:

"We need history."

The next question should immediately be:

"History of what?"

If the business needs the photograph, it needs evidence. If it needs to know what warehouse movement occurred, it needs execution history. If it needs to know who was responsible for the situation, it needs situation and responsibility information. If it genuinely needs an enterprise document-management lifecycle, DMS may become relevant.

The word history by itself is not enough to determine the technical solution.

This becomes especially important for audit requirements.

An audit question may be: What did the operator see? What evidence was captured? Who performed the action? When did it happen? What warehouse movement was executed? Why was the decision taken?

These questions describe different types of information.

Therefore: audit requirement does not automatically mean DMS.

The better question is:

"What story does the audit need to reconstruct?"

If that story is already represented across the business situation, business object, supporting evidence and execution history, another repository may simply duplicate information rather than solve a new requirement.

DMS becomes relevant when the business genuinely requires structured document-management capabilities beyond what the existing business objects and processes provide.

When the Pattern Changes

This approach does not mean that GOS should always be used, Situation Handling should always be used, or DMS should never be used.

The requirement determines the capability.

A transportation exception may require TM capabilities. A maintenance-related requirement may require EAM capabilities. A warehouse execution requirement may require EWM capabilities. A genuine enterprise document-management requirement may require DMS.

The technical objects change according to the business context. The reasoning does not:

Business Requirement → Natural Capability → Configuration → Integration where required → Custom Development only where a real gap remains

That is the reusable part of the approach.

No Custom Code as the Foundation

Standard SAP capabilities should be considered before introducing custom development.

The fact that several SAP capabilities are involved does not automatically mean that a custom layer is required. Sometimes the cleaner architecture is simply to let each standard capability perform the responsibility it already owns.

Technical Implementation: Ground to SAP

The business-first design eventually has to reach the SAP implementation layer.

For evidence, the design can use GOS / Attachment, where supported by the relevant business object or application.

For business attention, Situation Handling can be used according to the applicable scenario and configuration. Manage Situation Types (F2947) is the relevant Fiori application for configuring situation types in supported scenarios.

For physical warehouse movement, the existing EWM process and warehouse tasks remain responsible for execution.

For confirmed warehouse execution history, /SCWM/ORDIM_C is the relevant EWM reference in this design.

The exact configuration path can depend on the SAP release and the specific Situation Handling or EWM scenario. Therefore, technical references should be validated against the actual release and application rather than treated as one universal configuration path.

The technical layer comes after the business requirement has been understood.

The Manyat Principle

The purpose of Manyat Thinking is not to reduce the number of SAP components.

It is to avoid making one component responsible for requirements that naturally belong to different capabilities.

The principle is:

Start with the business requirement, identify the SAP capability that naturally owns it, and avoid adding another layer unless the requirement genuinely needs it.

And one question keeps the architecture honest:

"Record of what?"

Core Manyat Pattern: Ground Reality → Exception → WHY → Business Requirement → SAP Capability → Technical Implementation → Business Action

Conclusion

A broken seal may look like a small warehouse exception, but it can expose a much larger architecture problem when every requirement is pushed into one technical mechanism.

The cleaner approach is to separate the requirements.

Let GOS / Attachment handle supporting evidence where appropriate. Let Situation Handling bring the relevant business situation to the responsible user. Let EWM handle the physical warehouse execution. Let EWM execution records provide the warehouse execution history. And let DMS handle genuine document-management requirements when they actually exist.

The objective is not to remove SAP capabilities. The objective is to make each capability responsible for the problem it naturally owns.

Start from the ground. Ask WHY. Identify the real requirement. Then let SAP capabilities do what they are designed to do.

Manyat Thinking | Business First. SAP Second.

entry.title: A Better Shop Floor Starts Now
entry.content:
Part 1 and part 2 were largely about the strategic decisions at board level and the technical decisions in the architecture room. This final part is about something rather more immediate than either of those.

It is about the person who walks into the plant at six in the morning, checks how the overnight production run went, and starts their day with whatever the current system happens to give them. Sometimes that is enough to work with, but often it is not, and the workarounds that have grown up to fill the gap have become so familiar that most teams have simply stopped noticing they are there.

That is the part of this whole transition that does not get talked about nearly enough. It is not the architecture or the timeline that ultimately determines whether this change is worth making, it is the day-to-day experience of the people running production.

The tools have not kept up

SAP Manufacturing Integration and Intelligence and SAP Manufacturing Execution were built on technology that is now well over twenty years old, and in manufacturing terms that is a genuinely significant gap. The shop floors these platforms were originally designed for looked quite different from today’s, the expectations placed on operations teams were different, and the speed at which decisions needed to be made was different again.

What has not changed, oddly enough, is the expectation that the people running production will somehow bridge the distance between what the system shows them and what is happening on the floor in front of them. End-of-shift data consolidation, manual re-entry between systems, quality checks logged after the fact rather than embedded into the process itself, dashboards that finally become accurate at roughly the same moment nobody needs them anymore and these are the everyday realities that operations teams have quietly absorbed for years.

None of this reflects a failure of process or effort on the part of the people involved. These are limitations of the platform itself, and they carry a cost that rarely gets properly quantified precisely because it has become background noise that nobody thinks to measure.

What actually changes

SAP Digital Manufacturing is built around a fairly straightforward premise: the people running manufacturing operations should have the information they need at the moment they need it, without having to go looking for it. That sounds simple enough on paper, but the implications of actually delivering on it are considerable.

Production visibility shifts from retrospective to genuinely near live. Dashboards update in near real time, but increasingly the experience is also becoming conversational. With SAP's AI capabilities and Joule, supervisors and production teams can interact with manufacturing information more naturally, helping them identify issues, understand performance trends, and access relevant operational insights faster. Anyone with responsibility for what is happening on the floor can see the current state of production orders, work center status, and material availability without waiting for someone to compile a report.

Work instructions become part of the process itself rather than a document that lives somewhere alongside it. The process designer in SAP Digital Manufacturing delivers digital work instructions including images and video where they help directly to the operator at the point of execution. That matters for quality, for onboarding new operators, and for keeping things consistent across shifts, because the instruction and the step it applies to now exist in the same place at the same time.

Another important shift is the increasing integration between production equipment and manufacturing processes. In many environments, machines can receive production-related information directly from SAP Digital Manufacturing and return execution data, process parameters, and production results back into the process record. Operators remain at the center of execution, but they no longer need to manually capture every piece of information required for traceability. The result is a more complete digital history of how products were manufactured, greater process transparency, and faster access to the information needed for quality, compliance, and continuous improvement.

Quality stops being a downstream activity that happens after the fact. In-process quality inspections get embedded directly into production steps, triggered automatically, with the results flowing to SAP S/4HANA Quality Management in real time. The practical effect is that the quality team spends less time chasing data around and more time actually acting on it.

OEE becomes a tool rather than a report. Overall Equipment Effectiveness tracking is built in, downtime events get classified, and performance trends surface without anyone having to manually pull them together. When a line stops, the system already knows, and when a pattern starts to emerge over time, it becomes easier to identify recurring causes and address them before they have a broader operational impact. Operational visibility improves not only within production itself, but also across the wider manufacturing landscape.

The gap between the shop floor and the ERP system essentially closes. The result is not only better synchronization between systems. It is a closer connection between manufacturing operations and the broader business, helping teams make decisions based on the same information, priorities, and customer commitments.

Production order confirmations, goods movements, inventory postings, and quality results all move between SAP Digital Manufacturing and SAP S/4HANA automatically, which means the synchronization delays and manual re-entry that have historically sat between the plant, and the wider business simply go away.

The transition itself

A fair question at this point is what the changeover actually feels like for the people going through it, and the honest answer is that it takes some adjustment. Workflows that have been second nature for years will genuinely work differently in the new environment, and any transition program that pretends otherwise is not really serving its people well.

What makes the difference is how that change is managed, rather than whether the platform itself is any good. SAP and its partner ecosystem have built enablement programs specifically aimed at operations teams making this kind of move, and the ones that matter most in practice tend to be role-based learning paths through SAP Learning Hub structured around the work that production supervisors, quality engineers, planners, and operators actually do rather than around generic system training along with proper process simulation before go-live so that teams are not encountering the new system for the first time on the day it matters most, and dedicated hyper-care support in the weeks immediately after go-live to resolve questions quickly and keep adoption moving forward.

The goal of a well-run transition is that day one in SAP Digital Manufacturing feels manageable rather than overwhelming, and that outcome is genuinely achievable, but it requires the investment in people to be treated with the same seriousness as the investment in the technology itself.

A Platform that does not stand still

One of the more meaningful differences between SAP Digital Manufacturing and what it is replacing is harder to put on a feature list, because it is really about trajectory rather than any specific capability

Legacy SAP Manufacturing Integration and Intelligence and SAP Manufacturing Execution platforms are at the end of their development lifecycle. What they are today is essentially what they will be in 2027, because no new capabilities are coming, no new integrations are being built, and there is no roadmap ahead of them.

SAP Digital Manufacturing sits on the opposite side of that equation. It is a cloud product with an active development program, and its capabilities improve on a continuous release cycle without any of the upgrade projects that used to accompany that kind of change. What the platform can do in 2026 will be materially more than what it does today, and more again the year after that.

The roadmap continues to evolve with new capabilities across areas such as planning, quality, sustainability, asset performance, and traceability. The specific features matter, but the bigger point is that the platform continues to improve without the disruption of traditional upgrade projects.

The point is that operations teams working on SAP Digital Manufacturing are not just getting a better platform today. They are getting one that keeps getting better on its own, automatically, as part of the service they are already paying for.

Getting the transition right on the ground

Technology transitions ultimately succeed or fail at the operational level. The architecture can be perfectly sound and the project management admirably disciplined, but if the people closest to the process are not properly involved from the beginning, the gap between what was designed and what actually gets used tends to widen surprisingly quickly after go-live.

Three things consistently make the difference in my experience. The first is capturing how the floor runs before design work begins, every workaround, every informal step, every little process that has grown up outside the system over the years. That knowledge is rarely obvious to program teams arriving from the outside, and it is exactly the kind of thing that good system design needs to reflect if it is going to work in practice.

The second is identifying what really matters before the build starts, particularly the reports, dashboards, and KPIs that production and quality teams rely on every day. If these are not properly validated before go-live, the first few weeks on the new platform end up being spent rebuilding trust rather than building capability, which is not a position anyone wants to find themselves in.

The third is getting into the system early. Simulation and training opportunities are available well before go-live, and the teams that actually make use of them rather than waiting for formal training closer to the date arrive at cutover with genuine familiarity rather than surface-level awareness. That difference is visible on day one, and it tends to compound from there.

The bigger picture

Across all three parts of this series, the argument has been fairly consistent. The end of SAP NetWeaver’s mainstream maintenance is not an inconvenience to be managed and moved past but it is a defined moment to make a deliberate choice about what kind of manufacturing organization you intend to be on the other side of it.

Part 1 made the case for moving with intent rather than out of obligation. Part 2 laid out how a well-structured technical program actually comes together. Part 3 is really just the reminder that both of those things ultimately serve one purpose, which is giving the people running manufacturing operations better tools, better information, and a platform capable of keeping pace with where the industry is heading. Better manufacturing systems ultimately matter because they help organizations deliver consistently on the promises they make to customers, whether that means quality, delivery performance, compliance, or responsiveness.

That is what this transition is genuinely about.

Not a deadline, and certainly not a compliance checkbox, but an opportunity to build a better shop floor and a stronger manufacturing organization while there is still time to do it deliberately and do it well.

entry.title: Without the SAP Business Network, your AI is just guessing
entry.content:
I spend most of my week talking with companies about AI. And the conversation is almost always the same. Everybody wants agents. Everybody has a pilot running somewhere. And almost nobody has it doing real work in production yet.

For a while I assumed the blocker was the models, or the budget, or people being nervous about letting software make decisions. It is none of those. When you actually dig in, it comes down to one thing: the AI does not have the full picture. It can only see what is inside the company's own four walls. And in procurement and supply chain, that is maybe half of what matters.

No Business does Business alone

Think about your own operation for a second: You do not forecast alone. You do not build alone, ship alone, or get paid alone.

There are suppliers, carriers, contract manufacturers, and customers in almost every step. So when your shiny new AI agent only knows your side of the story, it is working half-blind. It knows what you ordered. It has no idea whether the supplier can actually ship it. It knows your plan. It knows nothing about the reality out in the network.

Trading Partners are everywhere in the process, not just at the edges

When I show companies where trading partners actually touch the process, the room usually goes quiet for a second. It is not one or two handoffs. It is the whole thing, start to finish.

There are many points of interaction with trading partners across supply chain and procurement processes

Plan and buy, make and deliver, operate and services, invoice and pay. Partners are in all of it. Forecasting, sourcing, confirming orders, receiving goods, tracking shipments, handling the invoice, chasing the exception when something goes wrong. Every one of those steps is also a place where things break. A missed update, a wrong quantity, a delay nobody saw coming.

And here is how most companies still run it

This is the part that always gets me. We are having serious conversations about autonomous agents, and a huge amount of this partner collaboration is still happening over email, phone calls, spreadsheets, EDI, and in some corners of the world, fax and paper.

Customer challenges when engaging with trading partners

The numbers tell the story. Seventy-one percent of procurement people say they get incomplete or fragmented information from their suppliers. Eighty-six percent of companies are still transacting with legacy methods. Seventy percent see legal and regulatory non-compliance as a real external risk.

You cannot build reliable automation on top of that. If every supplier sends data in their own format, through their own channel, no agent can act on it with confidence.

What SAP Business Network actually does

So this is where SAP Business Network, the world’s largest B2B trading platform, comes in, and I will keep it simple because the idea is simple. Instead of wiring yourself to each partner one connection at a time, you join one network where everyone already is.

One network to transact and communicate with all of your trading partners

One connection, and you can reach thousands of partners. Transactions, documents, discovery, collaboration, all in one place and in one language. For over fifteen years this has been running at scale, which matters, because that is fifteen years of partner data arriving structured, clean, and ready to use instead of trapped in somebody's inbox.

Why this is the real unlock for AI

Here is my actual point, and the reason I keep bringing SAP Business Network into every AI conversation I have.

With the Network, AI sees both sides. Only then is a process truly end-to-end

SAP has a strong story on the inside. Fifty years of process knowledge, a semantic model that gives data real business meaning, and governance that is certified and built in rather than bolted on. More than 120 mission-critical processes, millions of data fields in the Knowledge Graph, every AI workload under certified controls. That is real, and it is hard to match.

But all of that is still only your half. The Network is what brings in the other half, the trading partner data, in the same structured, governed way. That is the piece people keep forgetting when they plan their AI roadmap. They treat the network as a nice-to-have you get to later. I would flip it:

The network is the thing that makes the AI trustworthy in the first place. It is not the last step. It is closer to the first.

And it is already paying off for people

I am not asking anyone to take this on faith. The companies already on the SAP Business Network are seeing it in the numbers that leadership actually cares about.

Compelling and quantifiable customer benefits with SAP Business Network

Better on-time delivery, fewer stock-outs, lower inventory, faster invoice processing, fewer compliance headaches. These are not slideware promises, they are outcomes customers are reporting today. And they compound once the AI on top of that data starts doing the routine coordination for you.

Where supply chain orchestration fits

You are hearing a lot about supply chain orchestration right now, and it is worth connecting the dots, because it is the same argument in different words. Orchestration means your planning, sourcing, making, moving, and paying all talk to each other, so when something shifts in one place the rest of the chain adjusts instead of finding out three weeks later.

That only works if the data is connected across companies, not just inside yours.

IDC put real numbers on what buyers want from orchestration:

  • flexibility
  • a single platform
  • AI built in
  • and crucially, support for the supplier network

Their own research shows most chief supply chain and procurement officers rank responding to disruption as their top priority, yet only about a quarter feel their supply chain is actually connected end to end. That gap is the opportunity, and the network is how you close it. Orchestration is really the on-ramp to an autonomous supply chain, and you do not get on it without the external data.

More on orchestration across the supply chain: What is supply chain orchestration?  

So here is what I would do

If you have AI pilots that look great in the demo and then stall before production, do not start by blaming the model. Go look at your partner data first. Ask how much of it is still arriving by email, how much you would trust an agent to act on unsupervised, and how much you simply cannot see.

Then let's talk. I would genuinely enjoy walking through where your processes still run on one-to-one connections and what it would take to get that other half of your data working for you. That is the groundwork that makes everything else, the agents, the orchestration, the autonomous enterprise, actually hold up.

Because no business does business alone. And no AI should either.

  • SAP Business Network for Asset Collaboration (BNAC)
  • SAP Business Network for Supply Chain Collaboration (BN4SC)
  • SAP Business Network for Procurement (BN4P) & Business Network for suppliers

entry.title: SAP IBP Response & Supply: ein Vorsprung, den kein anderer einholt
entry.content:
SAP IBP Response & Supply: ein Vorsprung, den kein anderer einholt

Auftragsbasierte Supply-Planung, native SAP S/4HANA-Ausführung und der Weg zur autonomen Lieferkette

Das Wichtigste in Kürze

  • SAP IBP Response & Supply plant auf einzelnen Aufträgen und schreibt sie über Real-Time-Integration direkt nach SAP S/4HANA zurück - kein anderes Planungstool leistet so eine Reaktionsfähigkeit.
  • Mit den letzten 2026-Releases (2602 / 2605 / 2608) wird dieser Vorsprung weiter ausgebaut: harmonisiertes Szenariomanagement, AI-unterstützte Szenarioplanung mit Joule, Merkmalsbasierte Planung mit Mindesthaltbarkeit, Lieferantengesteuerte Bestandsführung (VMI), Intelligente Deployment Conversion, MM-Lieferpläne sowie Qualitätsprüflose zeigen die tiefe Integration mit der Execution.
  • Dasselbe Fundament macht agentische, autonome Supply-Planung real statt zur Demo: ein Agent, der auf echten Aufträgen handeln kann — kontrolliert und nachvollziehbar — innerhalb des Design-to-Operate-Prozesses von SAP.

Die meisten Supply-Chain-Planungstools beantworten die Frage „Wie viel sollen wir nächsten Monat produzieren?" SAP IBP Response & Supply beantwortet eine wertvollere Frage mit dem Kunden im Mittelpunkt: „Dieser konkrete Kundenauftrag wird sich um drei Tage verspäten — hier ist der genaue Grund, und was jetzt zu tun ist."

Das ist der Kern dessen, was Response & Supply schwer kopierbar macht — und die 2026-Releases (SAP IBP 2602, 2605 und 2608) bauen diese Alleinstellungsmerkmale von SAP IBP Response & Supply weiter aus.

________________________________________

Inhalt

 

1 Das Fundament — Auftragsbasierte Planung und native SAP S/4HANA-Integration

2 Die Gamechanger — Was 2026 den Vorsprung zementiert hat

3 Ausblick — Der Weg zur autonomen Supply Chain

________________________________________

 

Das Fundament: Auftragsbasierte Planung und native SAP S/4HANA-Integration

Wettbewerbsvorsprung durch auftragsbasierte Planung, eng verzahnt mit der Ausführung

Viele Supply-Chain-Planungstools planen in Zeitrastern und aggregierten Mengen. Dieser Ansatz hat echte Stärken — und SAP IBP bietet ihn nativ an: SAP IBP Time Series Supply Planning ist gezielt für Organisationen gemacht, die eine aggregierte Sicht wollen, bei der die Planung auf Perioden- und Gesamtmengenebene genau die richtige Flughöhe ist. Doch wenn eine Störung eintritt, können aggregierte Zahlen nur sagen, dass ein Bucket zu knapp ist. Sie können nicht sagen, welcher Auftrag gefährdet ist, welcher Kunde betroffen ist oder welche einzelne Restriktion der Auslöser ist.

Ein Beispiel, das diese Lücke gerade in Echtzeit illustriert: Am 5. Oktober 2026 wurden in der Straße von Hormus drei Tanker getroffen. Petrochemische Abnehmer und energieintensive Industrien weltweit wussten binnen Stunden, dass eine kritische Schifffahrtsroute zum Risiko geworden ist — aber die entscheidende Frage blieb offen: Welcher konkrete Lieferauftrag ist auf welchem Schiff, und welcher Produktionsplan hängt davon ab? Wer auf aggregierter Zeitrasterebene plant, sieht nur, dass ein Bucket knapp werden könnte. Wer auf Auftragsebene plant, kann genau diese Frage beantworten — und reagieren, bevor der Engpass die Fertigung erreicht.

Den Unterschied macht das einheitliche Datenmodell von SAP IBP. Beide Engines laufen auf denselben Planungsbereichen, Stammdaten und Kennzahlen — sodass kein Abgleich zwischen getrennten Tools notwendig ist. Kunden wählen für jeden Teil ihres Netzwerks die passende Flughöhe oder kombinieren beide, vollständig innerhalb einer Plattform. SAP IBP Response & Supply plant auf der Ebene einzelner Aufträge — Fertigungsaufträge, Bestellungen, Umlagerungen und Kundenaufträge. Zwei Eigenschaften, die einen strukturellen Vorteil schaffen:

1. Granularität auf Auftragsebene. Jedes Planungsergebnis lässt sich auf ein reales Auftragsobjekt abbilden. Ein Planer kann eine verspätete Lieferung bis zum exakten geplanten Zugang und dem exakten Material zurückverfolgen, das sie ausbremst.

2. Native SAP S/4HANA-Integration — keine Middleware. Response & Supply liest und schreibt reale SAP-Ausführungsobjekte direkt über Echtzeit-Integration (RTI). Planaufträge fließen zurück nach SAP S/4HANA und werden ausgeführt, ohne ETL-Schichten oder nächtliche Batch-Brücken. Kein Planungsanbieter kann das erreichen: Sie integrieren zu SAP über Batch-Extrakte und individuelle Middleware, während SAP IBP reale Ausführungsobjekte per bidirektionaler Echtzeit-Integration (RTI) live liest und schreibt — als Standardprodukt, nicht als selbstgebaute Brücke. SAP IBP nimmt über ein Integrationsframework mit offenen APIs Daten aus Nicht-SAP-ERPs und externen Quellen auf — heterogene Multi-ERP-Landschaften werden damit unterstützt, auch ohne tiefe Ausführungsanbindung an SAP S/4HANA.

Alles Folgende erweitert dasselbe Prinzip: präzise planen und das Ergebnis direkt an die Ausführung übergeben.

________________________________________

Zwei Differenzierungsmerkmale auf diesem Fundament

Ursachenanalyse auf Auftragsebene. Weil die Planung auf realen Aufträgen über die mehrstufige Stückliste hinweg stattfindet, kann ein Planer die Restriktion hinter einem konkreten verspäteten Auftrag genau bestimmen, statt auf einen aggregierten Fehlbestand zu starren. Das ist der Unterschied zwischen einem Nachmittag Recherche und einer Zwei-Minuten-Entscheidung.

Transport Load Builder (TLB). TLB fasst Deployment-Anforderungen zu optimierten Transportladungen zusammen, die reale Kapazitätsrestriktionen berücksichtigen — Gewicht, Volumen sowie Fahrzeug-/Palettengrenzen — und rundet sie auf volle LKW- oder Container-Mengen, damit Planer keine halbleeren LKW losschicken oder eine Route überbuchen. Entscheidend: TLB ist kein separates Optimierungs-Silo, sondern sitzt direkt auf auftragsbasiertem Deployment und nativer SAP S/4HANA-Ausführung — der Fluss läuft ununterbrochen von der Supply-Entscheidung über den Ladeplan bis zur ausgeführten Lieferung. Eigenständige Ladeplanungs-Tools gibt es; was ihnen fehlt, ist diese nahtlose Linie von der Supply-Entscheidung auf Auftragsebene bis zum beladenen LKW, in einem System.

________________________________________

Planner Workspace als zentrales Planungscockpit

Eine berechtigte Kritik an Enterprise-Planungssuiten — SAP eingeschlossen — war lange eine Anwendererfahrung der Planer, die über zu viele Bildschirme verteilt ist. SAP hat massiv investiert, um dem zu begegnen: Die Response-&-Supply-Oberflächen konvergieren zu Planner Workspaces als einem einzigen Planungs-Cockpit — einem One-Stop-Arbeitsplatz zum Erkennen, Entscheiden und Handeln. Auftragsprüfung, projizierter Bestand, Deployment, Engpassanalyse und Szenarioplanung leben zunehmend in einem konfigurierbaren Workspace, sodass ein Planer vom Erkennen eines Problems über das Simulieren einer Reaktion bis zum Freigeben der Aufträge kommt — ohne zwischen unverbundenen Apps zu springen. Weniger Kontextwechsel, eine konsistente Oberfläche. Und mit eingebettetem Joule erhält dieses Cockpit einen einzigen natürlichsprachigen Einstiegspunkt über diese Aufgaben hinweg — genau dort, wo der Planer arbeitet, bittet er die KI zu handeln. → Demo: Planner Workspaces – In-Focus Alerts (1:28)

________________________________________

Die Gamechanger: Was 2026 den Vorsprung zementiert hat

AI-Assisted Scenario Planning, auf harmonisiertem Szenariomanagement

SAP IBP 2602 führte harmonisiertes Szenariomanagement ein — ein einheitliches Modell, das Aufträge und Kennzahlen vereint, mit vollständigem Lebenszyklus (Anlegen, Ändern, Übernehmen) in Planner Workspaces. Dazu kamen Simulationen auf Basis von Auftragsszenarien, längere Szenariolaufzeiten, eine Übernahme, die nun auch Aufträge einschließt, und kontrolliertes Shine-Through für Aufträge. → Demo: Harmonized Scenario Management (3:23) → Release-Blog: SAP IBP 2602

SAP IBP 2608 setzt Joule als AI-Assisted Scenario Planning auf dieses Fundament. Per natürlicher Sprache kann ein Planer, der auf einen Lieferantenausfall reagiert, Joule bitten, die Auswirkung des Ausfalls bis hinunter zur Primärnachfrage zu bewerten, Aufträge für den betroffenen Lieferanten zu löschen, diesen Lieferanten von Planungsläufen auszuschließen und neuen Supply aus alternativen Quellen anzulegen — aus einer mehrstündigen manuellen Untersuchung wird ein geführter Dialog. Weil Szenarien auf realen Aufträgen operieren, zeigt der KI-Vergleich, welche konkreten Kundenaufträge jede Reaktion schützt oder opfert — nicht nur ein aggregiertes Service-Level-Delta. → Demo: AI-Assisted Scenario Planning (5:09) → Release-Blog: SAP IBP 2608

Merkmalsbasierte Planung für Prozess-, Pharma- und Nahrungsmittelindustrie

Planung auf SKU-Ebene reicht nicht, wo zwei Chargen des „gleichen" Produkts nicht austauschbar sind. SAP IBP 2602 kombinierte Merkmalsbasierte Planung mit Mindesthaltbarkeit: Mindesthaltbarkeit nach Merkmalen definieren, Verfallsdaten von Planungselementen wie Beständen berücksichtigen und die richtige Charge durch Bewertung von Merkmalen und Restlaufzeit auswählen — direkt auf Abfallreduktion und regulatorische Compliance in Food und Pharma ausgerichtet. SAP IBP 2608 ergänzte auch den SAP-Best-Practices-Content für CBP (auf Planungsbereich SAPIBP2, mit Prozess-/Konfigurations-/Test-Assets), sodass Bedarfe mit Merkmalen nur von passendem Supply erfüllt werden. Nur sehr wenige Planungsplattformen leisten das nativ.

Lieferantengesteuerte Bestandsführung (SAP IBP 2605)

SAP IBP 2605 führte Vendor Managed Inventory mit automatisierter Wiederbeschaffungsplanung ein. Statt dass der Kunde die Wiederbeschaffung anstößt, plant und triggert sie der Lieferant: Kundenbedarf und Bestandstransparenz speisen den SAP IBP-Supply-Planungslauf, Wiederbeschaffungsaufträge fließen automatisch über Echtzeit-Integration ins ERP, und ausnahmebasierte Alerts melden Probleme, ohne den automatisierten Fluss zu stören. Eine Koordinationsübergabe, die normalerweise in Tabellen und EDI lebt, läuft vollständig in derselben auftragsbasierten Engine. → Demo: Vendor-Managed Inventory (3:42) → Release-Blog: SAP IBP 2605

VMI ist zugleich der Einstieg in ein Thema, das Analysten und Wettbewerber stark gewichten — die mehrstufige Lieferantenkollaboration. Zusammen mit dem SAP Business Network reicht auftragsbasierte Planung über die Unternehmensgrenzen hinaus: Prognose-, Bestell- und Bestandssignale lassen sich mit Lieferanten upstream teilen, sodass der Plan widerspiegelt, was Partner tatsächlich zusagen können, statt einer internen Annahme.

Intelligent Deployment Conversion (SAP IBP 2602)

Ein neuer Deployment-Conversion-Algorithmus wandelt Umlagerungsanforderungen automatisch in Deployment-Anforderungen um und nutzt dabei ausschließlich verfügbaren Supply (verfügbarer Bestand, geplante Zugänge). Er wandelt nach Bedarfstermin-Priorität um — das Dringendste zuerst — mit konfigurierbaren Bedarfs- und Supply-Horizonten. Überfällige Elemente verschiebt er zeitlich zurück, fixierte Umlagerungsanforderungen bezieht er ein, und bei Teilverfügbarkeit teilt er sie — unter Wahrung der Rundungswerte — auf. Dieser Schritt verwandelt einen machbaren Supply-Plan in konkrete, ausführbare Aufträge — der natürliche Zulauf zu TLB und Ausführung. → Demo: Deployment Conversion Run (4:34)

Tiefere Integration in die native Ausführung (SAP IBP 2608)

Drei Supply-Erweiterungen bauen den Vorsprung weiter aus, indem sie reale SAP S/4HANA-Ausführungssignale in die auftragsbasierte Planung einbeziehen:

  • Qualitätsprüflose werden in Echtzeit aus ECC/SAP S/4HANA in SAP IBP integriert, sodass in der Prüfung gebundener Bestand (mit erwarteten Freigabedaten und -mengen) in Planungsläufen berücksichtigt wird.
  • MM-Lieferpläne bringen MM-Einteilungen über RTI in SAP IBP. Im SAP IBP werden Kundenbedarfe bestätigten Einteilungen zugeordnet, was die Volatilität im Plan senkt.
  • Zeitabhängige Ausbeute lässt Ausbeuteraten während der Stücklistenauflösung je Planungsperiode variieren — relevant für Halbleiter, Pharma, Food & Beverage, Chemie und diskrete Fertigung. → Demo: Time-Dependent Output Coefficient (3:34)

________________________________________

Beweis in der Praxis

Das ist nicht abstrakt — auftragsbasiertes Response & Supply ist produktiv im Einsatz:

  • BSH Hausgeräte setzt SAP IBP for Response & Supply ein, um die taktische Supply-Planung direkt mit Verfügbarkeitsprüfung zu verbinden. O-Ton des BSH-S&OP-Transformationsleiters: „With SAP IBP [...], we consistently combine the tactical operational planning with the actual execution of day-to-day business … allocation concepts to handle scarcity and to be much more reliable in what we tell our customers when it comes to order promising.“ Nach erfolgreichem Start in China rollt BSH Response & Supply unternehmensweit aus. (SAP News, BSH-Kundenstory)
  • Viessmann Climate Solutions hat auftragsbasierte Planung in SAP IBP Response & Supply mit Echtzeit-Integration (RTI) zu SAP S/4HANA umgesetzt — beschrieben als eine der weltweit ersten Implementierungen der regelbasierten Kundenauftragsbestätigung auf RTI, für stabile, verlässliche Auftragsbestätigungen in Echtzeit, mit Stammdaten- und Auftragssynchronisation zwischen SAP S/4HANA und SAP IBP. Ein direkter Beleg für genau den Vorsprung, den dieser Beitrag beschreibt: die auftragsbasierte Engine, nativ mit der Ausführung verdrahtet. (Success Story, via SAP-Partner CONSILIO)

________________________________________

Ausblick: Der Weg zur autonomen Supply Chain

Von KI-Assistenz zu agentischer Planung

Das AI-Assisted Scenario Planning aus SAP IBP 2608 stellt Joule als Copilot an die Seite des Planers: Der Planer fragt, die KI schlägt vor, der Planer entscheidet. Die Stoßrichtung ist agentisch — KI, die nicht nur antwortet, sondern proaktiv eine Störung erkennt, die auslösende Ursache diagnostiziert, Reaktionsszenarien entwirft, sie bewertet und die korrigierenden Aufträge zur Freigabe vorbereitet.

Hier wird auftragsbasierte Planung entscheidend, denn ein Agent ist nur so nützlich wie die Aktionen, die er tatsächlich ausführen kann. Da Response & Supply auf realen Aufträgen plant und sie direkt in die SAP S/4HANA-Ausführung zurückschreibt, kann ein Agent auf diesem Fundament mehr tun, als eine Empfehlung anzuzeigen — er kann alternativen Supply anlegen, knappen Bestand über konkurrierende Kundenaufträge umverteilen und Deployment- und Ladeentscheidungen zur Freigabe vorbereiten. Die „letzte Meile" von der Erkenntnis zur ausgeführten Aktion steckt nativ im System — sie ist kein nachgelagertes Integrationsprojekt. Genau das macht aus agentischer Planung mehr als eine Demo: präzise Entscheidungen auf realen Aufträgen, ausgeführt im System of Record.

Und weil jede Agentenaktion eine reale Auftragsänderung im System of Record ist, ist sie von Natur aus kontrollierbar und nachvollziehbar — zur menschlichen Freigabe vorbereitet, begrenzt durch dieselben Berechtigungen und Kontrollen wie jede andere Planungsaktion. Während Analysten zu Recht auf die Lücke zwischen angekündigter und vertrauenswürdiger Autonomie drängen, ist dieses kontrollierte, ausführbare Modell die substanzielle Antwort: nicht ein Agent, der redet, sondern einer, der innerhalb von Leitplanken handelt, die man inspizieren kann.

________________________________________

Was als Nächstes kommt: geplant für SAP IBP 2611

Die folgenden Punkte sind geplante Fähigkeiten auf der SAP-Roadmap für das Release SAP IBP 2611. Sie sind zukunftsgerichtet, können sich ändern und sind noch nicht allgemein verfügbar.

  • Kuppel- und Nebenprodukte — auftragsbasierte Supply-Planung, die Fertigungsprozesse mit mehreren gleichzeitigen Ausbringungen berücksichtigt, sodass Kuppel- und Sekundärprodukte kohärent geplant statt approximiert werden. Besonders relevant für Chemie, Raffinerie, Metalle und Food & Beverage — und eine natürliche Ergänzung zum Characteristics-Based Planning.
  • Transport Load Builder — Upsizing — erweitert TLB, um unterfüllte Ladungen zu einer wirtschaftlichen Volllast aufzubauen (etwa durch Vorziehen geeigneten Bedarfs), sodass LKW und Container gut ausgelastet statt teilbeladen fahren.
  • Transport Load Builder — Minimum Threshold — erlaubt Planern, ein Mindest-Füllniveau (Gewicht, Volumen oder Menge) zu definieren, unter dem eine Transportladung nicht freigegeben wird — vermeidet unwirtschaftliche Kleinlieferungen und setzt Ladeeffizienz-Richtlinien durch.

Diese Erweiterungen manifestieren das, wofür SAP IBP Response & Supply steht: Prozessindustrie-Tiefe und Ausführungsstärke.

________________________________________

Das größere Bild: ein Baustein von SAPs autonomem Unternehmen

Alles Obige weist in eine Richtung: SAPs Vision einer autonomen Lieferkette — ein System, das eine Veränderung erkennt, entscheidet, wie zu reagieren ist, handelt und lernt, während der Planer nach dem Ausnahmeprinzip überwacht, statt jede Transaktion zu steuern. Autonomie ist nur so vertrauenswürdig wie die Entscheidungen und Aktionen darunter — und genau dort verdient sich Response & Supply seinen Platz: präzise Entscheidungen auf realen Aufträgen, nativ im System of Record ausgeführt. Es ist das operative Fundament, auf dem die autonome Vision steht.

Drei Verbindungen machen Response & Supply zu einem Baustein statt zu einer Insel:

  • Teil eines End-to-End-Prozesses, kein Modul. Response & Supply ist der planerische Herzschlag von SAPs Design-to-Operate-Prozess — Plan, Manufacture, Deliver, Operate. Autonomie potenziert sich, wenn sie diese gesamte Kette umspannt: ein Plan, der ohne Nahtstellen in Fertigungs- und Logistikausführung und zurück fließt.
  • Von einem Agenten zu kollaborierenden Agenten. Die heutige Joule-assistierte Planung ist der erste Schritt zu mehreren spezialisierten Agenten, die prozessübergreifend zusammenarbeiten — ein Planungsagent, der sich mit Beschaffungs-, Fertigungs- und Logistikagenten abstimmt. Weil Response & Supply auf realen Aufträgen in SAP S/4HANA handelt, bringt sein Agent etwas mit, das beratende Agenten nicht können: die Fähigkeit, seinen Teil der Entscheidung tatsächlich auszuführen.
  • Fundiert auf einheitlichen Geschäftsdaten. Autonome Entscheidungen brauchen ein vertrauenswürdiges, geteiltes Datenfundament. Das einheitliche Planungsmodell in SAP IBP erstreckt sich nach außen auf SAPs breitere Datenstrategie — SAP Business Data Cloud und eine semantische Sicht auf das Geschäft — sodass Agenten über konsistente, kontrollierte Daten folgern.

Damit wird die Rolle des Planers neu definiert: weniger manuelles Feuerlöschen, mehr Orchestrierung und Ausnahme-Governance — ein Mensch, der einen autonomen Kreislauf überwacht, den er inspizieren, korrigieren und dem er vertrauen kann.

________________________________________

Das Fazit

Das wahre Alleinstellungsmerkmal ist kein einzelnes Feature — es ist die Kombination: auftragspräzise Planung, verschmolzen mit nativer SAP-Ausführung. Harmonisiertes Szenariomanagement, Joule-getriebenes AI-Assisted Scenario Planning, Characteristics-Based Planning mit Mindesthaltbarkeit, Vendor Managed Inventory, Intelligent Deployment Conversion und der Transport Load Builder sind jedes für sich stark. Zusammen, auf diesem Fundament, ergeben sie etwas, das kein anderer Planungsanbieter im SAP-Umfeld zusammensetzen kann.

Für jede Organisation auf SAP S/4HANA, die eine kurzfristige, störungsreaktive Supply-Planung braucht, die bis zur Laderampe reicht, gibt es schlicht kein Äquivalent. Und während SAPs Autonomous Enterprise Gestalt annimmt, ist dasselbe Fundament — präzise Entscheidungen auf realen Aufträgen, nativ ausgeführt — das, was aus der Vision einer selbstfahrenden Lieferkette etwas Greifbares macht.

________________________________________

Sie sind dran

Wo würde Autonomie Ihrer Lieferkette am meisten helfen — und wo möchten Sie den Menschen weiterhin fest am Steuer behalten? Ich bin gespannt, wie Sie auftragsbasierte Planung und agentische KI in Ihrem Netzwerk sehen.

  • Kämpft Ihre Planung noch mit aggregierten Buckets, während die eigentliche Frage lautet: Welcher Auftrag, welcher Kunde?
  • Können Sie in Echtzeit auf Änderungen in der Nachfrage reagieren und diese End-to-End bis auf den Truck-Load orchestrieren?
  • Wenn ein KI-Agent auf Ihrem Plan handeln könnte — nicht nur beraten — was würden Sie ihn autonom tun lassen, und was würden Sie zur Freigabe absichern?
  • Welche 2026-Fähigkeit ist für Sie am relevantesten: AI-Assisted Scenario Planning, Vendor Managed Inventory oder Characteristics-Based Planning?

Hinterlassen Sie einen Kommentar — und folgen Sie den Release-Ankündigungen für SAP IBP 2611.

________________________________________
