entry.title: Curiosity, Resilience and AI: What Leading CPOs Are Building Now
entry.content:
Curiosity, Resilience and AI: What Leading CPOs Are Building Now

Insights from The Future of Procurement podcast:  https://pod.link/1764078646

🎙️ Procurement’s future is not waiting on the horizon. It is taking shape in today’s decisions about artificial intelligence, supply resilience, talent, and business value. In a special episode of The Future of Procurement, Gordon Donovan, Vice President Research – Procurement & External Workforce at SAP, brings together perspectives from the chief procurement leaders of Nestlé, Kraft Heinz and Heineken. Their organizations face different category dynamics, yet their messages converge around a powerful idea: procurement can turn disruption into advantage when technology is paired with judgment, curiosity and commercial confidence.

Curiosity is becoming a core procurement capability

🔎 Across all three conversations, curiosity emerged as more than a desirable behavior. It is becoming an operating requirement. Procurement teams must continually scan geopolitical developments, weather patterns, commodity markets, tariffs, supplier conditions, and new technologies. The professionals who experiment, ask better questions and challenge assumptions are better positioned to identify threats early and uncover opportunities that a narrow, transactional view would miss.

💡 This matters because volatility is now persistent rather than exceptional. A change in crop conditions can affect cocoa or coffee availability. A tariff decision can alter the economics of a sourcing origin overnight. Curiosity enables teams to connect these external signals with category strategies, product requirements, and the company’s growth agenda. For leaders, the practical implication is clear: create structured opportunities for people to explore AI, test scenarios and share what they learn, rather than leaving adoption to a few enthusiasts.

AI should amplify judgment, not put procurement on autopilot

🤖 The CPOs described meaningful AI progress in productivity use cases, including contract summarization, data cleansing, planning, content creation and process guidance. The next horizon is more ambitious: agentic workflows, hands-free procurement experiences, and AI support for category strategy. These capabilities can reduce transactional effort and give professionals more capacity for supplier relationships, market intelligence, and strategic decision-making.

⚠️ But the episode also draws an important boundary. AI output cannot become an instruction that people accept without scrutiny. Contracts, sourcing choices and category recommendations still require business context, critical evaluation, and accountability. “Human in the lead” is therefore not resistance to automation. It is a design principle: let technology assemble information, surface patterns and accelerate routine work, while skilled people test the logic and own the decision.

Resilience and cost are not opposing choices

🛡️ The traditional debate frames resilience as an added cost: dual sources, inventory buffers, alternate origins and qualified backup sites all require investment. The leaders in this episode offer a more strategic view. The real question is where resilience produces the greatest return relative to risk and competition. A company does not need every item dual sourced. It needs a fact-based view of criticality, exposure, recovery options, and the commercial consequences of interruption.

📈 That leads to targeted resilience. Teams can pre-qualify multiple supplier locations, develop local and imported options, adapt formulations where appropriate, and document contingency actions before a crisis. Some preparation costs little until activated, yet it can materially improve response speed. The competitive benefit is not merely avoiding disruption. It is absorbing volatility more smoothly than peers and protecting availability, margins and customer preference.

Procurement value must connect to business strategy

🤝 Cost discipline remains essential, but world-class procurement communicates value in the language of the enterprise. Savings can fund brand investment and growth. Supplier partnerships can accelerate innovation and sustainability. Better contracts can protect flexibility and reduce risk. Strong market insight can inform pricing, planning, and investment decisions. The function earns influence when it understands the business strategy, builds confidence with senior stakeholders, and speaks up with a clear point of view.

🌱 The talent model must evolve with that mandate. As shared services, robotics and AI absorb more transactional work, teams will need stronger business partnering, storytelling, influencing and strategic judgment. Leaders should reinvest a portion of technology-enabled efficiency into capability building, ensuring that a potentially smaller organization is also more skilled, externally aware and effective.

A leadership call to action

🚀 Procurement leaders should ask three questions now:

  1. Are we deliberately building curiosity?
  2. Have we defined where AI assists and where people must decide?
  3. Are resilience investments tied to critical business outcomes and competitive position?

The organizations that answer these questions with discipline will be better equipped to convert uncertainty into sustainable value.

📣 To explore how SAP can help your organization modernize procurement, strengthen resilience and apply AI responsibly, connect with SAP. Then listen to this episode of The Future of Procurement podcast for the full conversations and subscribe to the show for more perspectives from the leaders shaping what comes next.  The Future of Procurement podcast:  https://pod.link/1764078646

entry.title: Migrating to SAP IBP Harmonized Planning Area (I_SAPIBP2): Before Getting Started
entry.content:
Earlier this year, SAP rolled out a comprehensive enablement program as part of the 2025–2026 migration strategy to ensure SAP IBP customers and partners confidently adopt the new Harmonized Planning Area (I_SAPIBP2),

SAP IBP’s HPA 2026 Strategy: Unified Planning and ... - SAP Community

With the release of the Migrate Configuration app (2605 release), SAP can support migrating existing IBP customers with SAP7F- or SAP7-based order-based planning areas to I_SAPIBP2 (HPA). The blog below contains some of the important technical pre-requisites with important tips and FAQs to help you kick-start with your HPA Brownfield migration journey from SAP7 or SAP7F.

SAP has developed a comprehensive Migration Guide specifically designed for moving from existing OBP planning areas to the Harmonized Planning Area (HPA). The guide is currently available to SAP consultants and SAP partners working with customers on HPA migration projects.

Pre-Requisites: Before Getting Started

  1. Know Your Migration Path

Before anything else, it is critical to identify which planning area you are migrating from, as this determines the complexity and the steps involved:

2. RTI Setup — Critical If You Are on SAP7 with SDI

Start with the S/4HANA side first. S/4HANA system upgrades — service packs or specific support notes — may be required. As seen earlier, it can take a long time for customers on older S/4HANA or ERP versions to install all required SAP Notes.  Note 3106619 - SAP IBP Real-time integration - Notes for installation - SAP for Me describes which support packages or notes you need to implement, depending on your release. The linked report CIF_NOTE_IMPL_SUPPORT_IBP will help identifying necessary notes.

You can use a dummy planning area (an independent copy of I_SAPIBP2 planning area) as a target for the RTI integration profile, so you can start RTI enablement before migrating the source planning area.

SAP provides a web-based application called CIAS (Cloud Installation Agent Support) that helps accelerate the setup of the Cloud Connector and all related connections as a kind of workflow.

Before starting with the move from SDI to RTI, make yourself familiar with the following information:

RTI Central Note: 3110007 - IBP Real-time Integration: Information/Restrictions - SAP for Me

3. Time Profile — The Most Critical Configuration Element

The time profile is one of the most important aspects of HPA migration. There are four specific areas related to the time profile to assess and resolve before proceeding:

  • Custom Time Profile Levels

Check your planning area's time profile for any custom (user-defined) levels — for example, a fiscal year structure or custom quarter definitions.

  • Additional Attributes on Time Profile Levels

Check whether your time profile levels have additional custom attributes assigned.  You need to attach them to the target time profile BEFORE the migration as well.

  • Plan for Future Merging of Planning Areas.

Consider whether you plan to merge multiple planning areas (e.g., order-based and time-series-based) now or in the future. Define the time profile with the union of all levels from all planning areas that may eventually be harmonized. Adding levels later is not possible. Adding attributes to existing time profile levels can be done at any time, but it is recommended to do that BEFORE the migration and before you load any data into the target time profile.

  • Understand How Your Period IDs Were Created

The Period ID (a technical identifier for each time period) is used internally across planning views, filters, and all other objects. The Migrate Configuration app currently assumes a one-to-one mapping of Period IDs between source and target. If you are unsure how your time profile was originally created (SAP standard numbering, manual upload, custom job), download the time profile CSV from the Data Integration app and share it with SAP Support via ticket.

4. Assess Your CI-DS Integration Strategy

 CI-DS (Cloud Integration Data Services) is supported for use with I_SAPIBP2. However, there are important nuances to evaluate before migration:

  • Existing CI-DS extractors used with SAP7 or SAP7F need to be tested and likely modified to conform with the I_SAPIBP2 data model.
  • Alternatively, this migration project is an opportunity to switch from CI-DS to SAP Integration Suite Cloud Integration (CI), where predefined CI data flows are provided to supplement RTI.

The choice between continuing with CI-DS and adopting CI is a strategic decision that involves both effort and long-term benefits. This decision should be made before the planning area migration begins.

CI-DS advantages

  • Preserves past investment in integration architecture and staff skills
  • Lower future integration license cost
  • Fastest and lowest risk HPA migration project
  • Ongoing SAP support (but no new features as IBP’s use of CI-DS is in maintenance mode)

CI advantages

  • SAP strategic integration platform with active roadmap and support
  • Used by most SAP products, making staff skills transferrable to other projects (CI-DS is used by IBP only)
  • IBP roadmap includes CI-specific features, in line with new HPA capabilities
  • Supports cloud to cloud integration (no on-prem agent required)

Migration FAQs

 In Addition to the above prerequisites, it's helpful to review some frequently asked questions (FAQs) from the early adopter program initiative.

 

Question

Response

How can we raise access to the Migrate Configuration app for migration to an I_SAPIBP2-based planning area, as SAP Help states that this is currently an Early Adopter feature?

To get access to the Migrate Configuration app, an incident must be raised via component SCM-IBP-CNF-M2F. The incident will be analyzed for appropriate project type and prerequisite skills.

Will CI-DS continue to work with HPA? Since CI-DS targets a specific planning area, do all CI-DS interfaces need to be modified?

Yes, CI-DS can continue with I_SAPIBP2, but existing CI-DS extractors are based on the SAPIBP1 and SAP7F data models. To use CI-DS with I_SAPIBP2, you must modify your own content. Alternatively, use this migration project as an opportunity to switch to SAP Cloud Integration with predefined data flows.

We are migrating from SAP7F and already have RTI in place with custom planning levels in OBP. Do we need to recreate those custom objects for the new planning area?

No. All configurations — custom key figures, planning levels, attributes — are supported by the Migrate Configuration app. Having RTI already in place will significantly accelerate the process. Some manual pre- and post-migration adjustments will be needed before the planning area activates.

We migrated from SAP7 to SAP7F and now want to go to I_SAPIBP2. Do we need to predefine all future time profile-level attributes, or can they be defined later?

Time-profile-level attributes can be added later, but it is recommended to add them before the migration. What cannot change is the structure and order of the time profile levels themselves (which determines the internal period ID numbering).

Does the existing HPA support subnetwork planning in OBP, or is that a future roadmap item?

Yes, subnetwork planning is currently available in OBP. The 2611 subnetwork item is specifically for time series supply optimization — not OBP.

Does the migration guide/app provide field-level mappings — specifically, old SAP7F attribute IDs mapped to their HPA counterparts?

Yes. The Migrate Configuration app contains all mappings in table form.

Historical data/KPIs — is there an automated tool for preserving them, or is it manual?

Data migration is not supported by Migrate Configuration app, but best practices are described in the migration guide. For example, if KPIs are stored as key figures in the old planning area, with equivalent key figures in the target, set up a copy operator to copy data from the source to the target, with attribute mappings defined between the two planning areas.

Our SAP7F is a non-cached version. Do we need to manually update the data source for each key figure to use cached data?

For SAP standard SAP7F key figures: no change needed. Only custom key figures with non-standard external data sources that reference non-cached order key figures need manual updates after migration to point to the cached data source.

I_SAPIBP2 has cached key figures built in — so we don't need to switch them on separately, right?  (Are these the OKF Keyfigures?)

Correct. Cached order key figures are enabled by default in I_SAPIBP2. It is a one-way setting — you cannot revert from cached back to non-cached.

Can two different forecast key figures be assigned to two different planning levels (one at product-location-customer level, another at product-location level)?

Yes, technically. The allocation profile and forecast consumption profile configured per product determine which level the system reads for each product. If it worked in SAP7F, it would work in I_SAPIBP2.

Can we add custom attributes now to time series planning levels in an existing live I_SAPIBP2 planning area that was set up for a different purpose?

Yes. Adding non-root attributes to an existing planning area is possible.

We have a live time series planning area and a live OBP planning area. The plan is to first migrate OBP, then merge time series 1.5–2 years later. Will that be possible?

Yes, this is the merge migration scenario for the Migrate Configuration app, which will be supported in 2027. The key prerequisite today: the time profile in the I_SAPIBP2 target must contain all time profile levels from both planning areas before the first migration, and it is recommended to contain all attributes then as well (not mandatory).

My Migrate Configuration app view looks different from what you are demonstrating, and I don't see the same grouped options.

You are missing the new business catalog that enables the enhanced grouped UI. If access was requested some time ago, the catalog may not have been assigned. Raise an SAP support ticket to have the new business catalog enabled. With release 2608, it will be automatically available in all systems.

If I made a mistake in the mapping, can I delete the profile, create a new one, and restart?

Yes. You can reuse an existing mapping profile in a new migration project or create a new one.  However, restart before making any manual adjustments to the target. If manual adjustments were already made and you re-run migration, those adjustments will be overwritten.

We have an active RTI profile for SAP7F. Can we create a second RTI profile for the new I_SAPIBP2 planning area while both connect to the same S4/ERP system simultaneously?

Yes. You need two different logical systems in S4 (SM59) — one per planning area. Inbound integration can run in parallel from the same ERP to both planning areas. Outbound integration must NEVER run from two planning areas simultaneously for the same data. Separate logical systems also help distinguish body logic between SAP7F and I_SAPIBP2 in your BADI development, as the data structure has changed and some BADI might need to be adjusted (e.g. on PDS).

There are ~200 OSS notes required for RTI setup in ECC. Should those be implemented before CIAS setup, or can they go in parallel?

They can mostly go in parallel. For most systems newer than ERP 6.0, ~95% of CIAS setup can proceed in parallel with note implementation.

We have custom staging tables in SDI that contain transformed data feeding into EXT tables. Can we reuse those custom staging tables as data sources in RTI BADIs?

Yes. Custom Z tables or standard X tables can be used as sources in RTI BADI logic.

I want to migrate content in stages (planning filters first, then analytics, etc.) while making changes to the target in parallel. Will re-running migration reset the target to the source state?

Yes. Re-running migration overwrites objects in the target. Make all changes in the source first, then migrate. Do not modify the target expecting those changes to survive a subsequent run of the Migrate Configuration app.

Does cross-planning-area (inter-planning-area) copy operator migration also work, or only within-planning-area ones?

Yes, inter-planning-area copy operators are also supported, with restrictions. Only copy
operators assigned to the source planning area (where the job is not executable from target) are supported.

Roles and authorizations — if copy operators or application job templates get new IDs after migration, do the role assignments get migrated too, or need to be recreated?

Business roles are not touched by the migration. Any role referencing technical names of application job templates or copy operators must be manually updated.

Does the Migrate Configuration app support a three-tenant IBP architecture?

No change. ATO (Advanced Transport Organizer) handles three-tier landscapes as standard.

We have a custom attribute-as-key-figure used in many calculations. In the source it is simple external master data type, but the target mapping points to a reference master data type. How do we add this attribute to the target?

Two options:

(1) Add the attribute-as-key-figure to the simple master data type and make it available in the reference master data type; define the key figure base level accordingly.

(2) Create a simple master data type with the same primary key as the reference master data type; add the custom attribute there; add this MDT together with the attribute to the planning level — the system will find it via shared key.

We cannot reuse the SAP7F RTI integration profile for I_SAPIBP2, correct?

Correct. Do not reuse the SAP7F RTI profile for I_SAPIBP2. Run the two workstreams in parallel: RTI provisioning (with notes) and HPA planning area configuration — no data flow needed during configuration phase.

We cannot create I_ key figures manually. How do we get SAP standard key figures from a new release into our existing HPA planning area?

Two options:

(1) Make a new copy of I_SAPIBP2 (sample template), then use the compare functionality to select specific key figures and merge them into your planning area.

(2) Use the new "partial merge" functionality in 2608 from the Sample Model Entity app.

The source attribute has a decimal data type but the I_SAPIBP2 target attribute is integer (e.g., frozen distribution horizon). Can we change the data type in the target? Can we increase the attribute length?

Data type changes: only possible before activation. Once activated, data types cannot be changed.

Attribute length changes: strongly discouraged. Any attribute in application mapping or RTI has strict length/type requirements. Changing field length or data type of standard attributes can cause activation and integration failures.

Can disabling the new uppercase-only setting on a target attribute cause activation errors?

No. There is no activation check on the uppercase setting. It is only a data consistency control.

After migrating to I_SAPIBP2, some calculated key figures take longer to refresh in planning views than they did in SAP7F. Are there best practices for performance in I_SAPIBP2?

Standard key figures should not be slower in I_SAPIBP2 than in SAP7F. For calculated key figures, the cause is likely a configuration issue.

When transporting the planning area to quality/production — how does the migration profile know the planning area step is done? Do we need to manually mark it as successful in QA/prod?

Yes. After transporting the planning area, application mapping, and migration profile to the next tenant, manually set the planning area migration step to "success" there. Then migrate remaining objects — especially non-transportable ones (e.g., planning filters created by planners directly in Excel in that system).

We have a SAP7F config planning area and a production planning area. Does the Migrate Configuration app mandate the same two-layer architecture?

Not mandatory. You can migrate using only the production planning area as source. If the config  planning area is always ahead (new features developed there) and production lags, migrating config first is easier.

You can then copy the migrated planning area, create a new migration project to it, assign your custom mapping profile and manually set the planning area to success. Then you can start migrating other objects such as excel planning view favorites that might only exist in the second planning area.

We are currently migrating OBP SAP7F. In a few months we may want to add demand planning to the same HPA planning area. Since demand migration requires the target not be productive, how does that work once OBP is live? What is the timeline for tool support?

SAP is enhancing the Migrate Configuration app for brownfield migration from SAPIBP1 to I_SAPIBP2. App support of “merge migration” scenarios will follow in 2027. (Merge migration moves SAPIBP1 or SAP7/7F source configuration into a preexisting I_SAPIBP2 planning area.)

In the meantime, projects can manually update their I_SAPIBP2 planning area to include time-series operators (demand, inventory, TS supply), or wait for merge migration app support in 2027.

 

Happy Reading! 🙂

entry.title: What’s New in Transportation Management of SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition 2025 - FP02
entry.content:
Today the latest Feature Package 02 (FP02) of SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition 2025 and SAP S/4HANA 2025 OP was released.

The latest innovations in SAP Transportation Management in SAP S/4HANA Private Cloud 2025 Feature Pack 2 highlights many enhancements that improve flexibility, transparency, and external collaboration in Freight Order Management as well as improve planning accuracy, usability, and flexibility across transportation processes. . There are quite a number of innovations in the area of clean core that support the clean-core concept and extensibility.

Lets first have a look into

Freight Order Management

Authorization to resolve freight document blocks

The first enhancement introduces a new Business Add-In (BAdI) that enables customers to define who is authorized to overrule or delete freight document blocks. Previously, any user with edit authorization could remove planning, execution, or invoicing blocks. With the new enhancement, organizations can implement their own authorization logic—for example, restricting compliance-related block overrides to specific key users—without modifying the standard application.

 

Result of the authorization check implemented in the BAdI

 

Processing and parking of reported external events

Another major improvement addresses event reporting from external applications such as SAP Business Network for Logistics or from EWM.
Instead of rejecting events that cannot be processed because of missing predecessor events or execution blocks, SAP TM now parks these events and provides clear document errors directly within the freight document. This gives business users full visibility into the issue, allows them to resolve problems without technical message monitoring tools, and automatically reprocesses parked events once blocking conditions have been resolved.

 Display of parked events and related actions

 

Support of external planning for star-shaped freight orders

The third mayor innovation is an enhancement for external planning, which is very important for many customers that let freight orders for instance plan by their carriers for instance in hub based pickup scenarios . SAP TM now fully supports the creation, update, and cancellation of star-shaped freight orders through standard external planning interfaces. This extends existing external planning capabilities to scenarios where detailed routing information remains with the carrier while allowing shippers to benefit from simplified freight order management. The enhancement delivers greater consistency across external planning processes while preserving the specialized behavior of star-shaped freight orders.

Enhancements in reporting of greenhouse gas emissions

Feature Pack Stack 2 further strengthens Transportation Management's sustainability capabilities by extending the inbound transportation event interface to support the reporting of actual greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Carriers can now submit verified emission values and their corresponding units of measure at either the freight order header or individual stage level, providing greater flexibility for real-world emissions reporting. When emissions are reported at the document level, SAP TM transparently distributes the values across stages for analytical purposes while preserving the original reported value at the document level. These enhancements simplify the integration of carrier-provided emissions data and support more accurate sustainability reporting within transportation processes.
For more detailed information please have a look at following blog post: Reporting of GHG emissions

  Emissions reported by the carrier and display in the freight order document

 

Filtering of Product Hierarchies

This Feature Pack also introduces new extensibility options that significantly improve how product and package hierarchies are processed during SAP Transportation Management (TM) integration. The new functionality addresses a long-standing challenge in integrated logistics processes, where different applications require different representations of the same business document.

Sales kits created in SAP SD are typically expanded into hierarchical item structures. While this level of detail is required for order processing, it is often not the optimal representation for transportation planning or warehouse execution. Depending on the business scenario, TM may only require the top-level kit item, while in other cases only the shippable components are relevant. Similar challenges exist for multi-level package hierarchies.

FPS2 introduces new and enhanced Business Add-Ins (BAdIs) that allow customers to control these hierarchy representations in a clean-core compliant manner. A new hierarchy filtering method enables independent filtering of both product and package hierarchies, allowing customers to retain only top-level items, only the lowest-level items, or the complete hierarchy. This filtering is applied within the logistics integration flow, enabling each consuming application to receive the representation that best matches its business requirements.

Hierarchy levels can be filtered on different levels based on customer needs

The enhancement also covers TM-induced delivery split scenarios. A new BAdI provides the necessary extensibility to adjust hierarchy information before it is transferred back to SAP Extended Warehouse Management (EWM), ensuring that both systems remain synchronized even when they operate on different hierarchy representations.

Beyond improving functional flexibility, the new extensibility helps reduce unnecessary document complexity and data volume, particularly in scenarios involving deeply nested packaging structures. Most importantly, the solution is fully upgrade-safe and clean-core compliant, replacing the implicit enhancements that many customers have relied on in previous releases.

With these enhancements, FPS2 provides a standardized and maintainable framework for adapting product and package hierarchy handling to individual business processes while preserving seamless integration between SAP SD, LE, TM, and EWM.

 

Means of Transport and Equipment Type Determination with consistent E2E usage in planning & optimization

A major focus is the enhanced Means of Transport (MTR) and Equipment Type Determination, and consitent usage through manual and automatic planning processes.

The innovation spans from order management into planning in an E2E manner.

With Feature Pack 2, SAP Transportation Management significantly extends the Means of Transport (MTR) determination introduced in FP01. While the original functionality was limited to Transportation Requirement Scheduling (TRS), the new release integrates MTR and equipment type determination consistently across the complete transportation planning process.

The key innovation is the introduction of a new condition type that determines not only means of transport and vehicle types, but also equipment types such as container types. This information can now be determined and persisted already on the Freight Unit stage as Preferred Means of Transport and Preferred Equipment Type, providing planning components with consistent guidance throughout the entire planning process.

The new functionality closes a long-standing gap between order scheduling and operational transportation planning. Previously, sales order scheduling could produce transportation proposals that were not reproducible during manual or optimizer-based freight unit planning, potentially resulting in inconsistent delivery commitments. Now, manual planning, optimizers, scheduling, default route determination, and load planning all leverage the same transportation preferences and determination logic, ensuring much more consistent planning results.

End-To-End usage of Preferred Means of Transport and Preferred Equipment Type

Another major enhancement is the seamless propagation of preferred means of transport and equipment types from Freight Units into Freight Orders and Container Units. At the same time, planners retain full flexibility, as automatically determined values remain transparent and can be manually overridden whenever required.

The enhanced determination logic has also been integrated into core planning components, including Lane Distance and Duration Determination (LDDD), Embedded Scheduling, the VSR Optimizer, Transportation Proposal, Load Consolidation, and Load Utilization Determination. Depending on the planning component, the system either consumes persisted preferred values or dynamically executes the determination at runtime. This enables planning decisions to consider transportation constraints much earlier while reducing the solution space for optimization algorithms and improving planning efficiency.

To support these capabilities, the Transportation Cockpit has been enhanced with new fields displaying preferred means of transport, equipment types, their origin, and editing capabilities. In addition, planning profiles now offer a dedicated configuration for the new determination logic. It is also recommended adopting the new equipment type condition type for new implementations, as it provides greater flexibility and is intended to replace the previous vehicle type determination approach over time.

Overall a much more comprehensive, rule-based transportation planning concept is introduced. By making transportation and equipment preferences available throughout the planning lifecycle, SAP TM delivers more consistent planning results, improved optimizer performance, greater transparency for planners, and better alignment between sales order scheduling and transportation execution.

 

Now lets have a look into the innovations that are introduced in other area's of

Planning & Network

Transportation Management continues to enhance planning capabilities with a strong focus on automation, planning accuracy, and flexibility. The latest innovations span Freight Unit Building, Unified Package Building, Load Planning, and Capacity Planning, helping customers model increasingly complex logistics scenarios while reducing implementation effort and the need for custom enhancements.

The release delivers important improvements in scheduling. As an example the Appointment validation has been corrected to provide more accurate error messages, and loading and unloading activities must now be scheduled completely within the appointment window instead of only partially overlapping. These changes help create more realistic and reliable transportation schedules.

Appointment Handling during scheduling

Scheduling Result takes into account appointments

In addition, the Explain Scheduling Results app has received usability enhancements, including a more efficient grid-based table and the ability to open detailed scheduling analyses in separate browser tabs.

 

More Accurate Freight Unit Building

Freight Unit Building now applies an improved packing heuristic based on the First Fit Decreasing algorithm. Compared to the previously used approach, the new heuristic achieves better capacity utilization by reducing unused space within freight units. As a result, fewer freight units are created while overall planning quality improves. An additional benefit is improved runtime performance, making Freight Unit Building both more efficient and more scalable for large planning scenarios.

 

Unified Package Building Becomes More Powerful

One of the most significant innovations in FPS2 is the continued enhancement of the Unified Package Building Optimizer (PBO).

The optimizer now supports auxiliary packaging materials such as packaging materials, separation materials, and cover materials when building layered pallets. These materials are no longer treated merely as additional objects but are considered during the optimization itself, including their physical position within the pallet structure. Consequently, pallet dimensions, weight, and stacking characteristics are represented much more accurately, leading to improved vehicle utilization and more reliable downstream planning.

Cover Material and Separation Materials are displayed in the hierarchy and the 3D scene

Customers can define detailed rules controlling when auxiliary packaging materials are inserted—for example after product changes, after a configurable number of layers, below consolidation layers, or as protective cover materials. The optimizer also determines their exact placement within the pallet, enabling highly realistic package structures for automated warehouse and transportation processes.

Besides improving planning accuracy, this enhancement eliminates many customer-specific workarounds that previously had to compensate for limitations in standard package building.

 

Flexible Package Building Through Condition-Based Configuration

Another major innovation is the introduction of a new condition-based framework for Package Building parameter determination.

Instead of relying solely on static Package Type Assignment settings, package building behavior can now be determined dynamically based on business process and document attributes. Different package building settings can therefore be applied depending on planning process, business document type, transportation characteristics, products, transportation zones, or customer-specific attributes.

The new framework introduces dedicated condition types, data access definitions, and an extensible plug-in concept that allows Transportation Management to determine package building settings at runtime. This significantly increases flexibility while reducing the amount of custom ABAP enhancements that were previously required to implement customer-specific packaging rules.

 

Enhanced Unified Package Building Test Cockpit

The Unified Package Building Test Cockpit also receives several important usability improvements.

Nested packaging hierarchies can now be visualized completely within the integrated 3D scene, allowing planners to inspect multiple packaging levels, from pallets down to individual cartons and their contents. Interactive highlighting simplifies navigation through complex packaging hierarchies, while document-based entry points can directly load package building results that already exist in business documents, avoiding unnecessary recalculation.

Test Cockpit for the Unified Package Builder

 

Together, these enhancements make it significantly easier to analyze optimization results, validate package building configurations, and troubleshoot complex packaging scenarios.

 

Better Manual and Automated Load Planning

Load Planning has also been enhanced in several areas.

For manual planning, labels displayed within the 3D load planning scene no longer interfere with drag-and-drop operations. Planners can now reposition freight while keeping all relevant information visible throughout the planning process, making manual load planning faster and more intuitive.

The optimizer has also been enhanced to better support mixed inbound and outbound transportation scenarios. Previously, combined delivery and return scenarios often required customer-specific developments. FPS2 introduces new configuration options that allow inbound or outbound items to be selectively ignored during optimization while remaining visible in both the planning hierarchy and 3D visualization. This provides greater flexibility for return logistics and mixed transportation scenarios without sacrificing transparency.

Visualization and hiding of items based on inbound or outbound scenarios

 

Incremental Creation of Capacity Documents Improves Automation

Capacity planning becomes considerably more intelligent with support for incremental creation of capacity documents based on groups.

Instead of always creating new freight orders when additional freight units become available, the system can now automatically evaluate existing freight orders and assign new freight units whenever sufficient capacity remains while respecing grouping criteria. Only when no suitable capacity is available will additional freight orders be created.

Adding of requirements to existing documents or creation of new capacity documents (based on groups)

This incremental planning approach improves vehicle utilization, reduces manual planning activities, and supports a more automated execution process while continuing to respect grouping criteria and capacity constraints.

 

Creation of Capacity Documents with Default Routes as a New Grouping Criterion 

Another planning innovation extends the grouping capabilities used during the creation of capacity documents.

Default routes can now serve as grouping criteria, allowing freight units that share identical routing characteristics to be consolidated automatically into the same freight order. Since default routes already encapsulate important transportation information such as transportation mode and routing decisions, this provides a powerful foundation for additional automated planning scenarios.

 

Invoicing Carrier and  Carrier Invoicing Level for Rail Freight Orders

Another innovation is particularly important for the rail business in North America, especially with regard to Rule 11. While the rail freight order already supported the invoicing carrier and the invoicing carrier level at stage level, this information can now also be maintained in the related default route. So far the maintenance of this data in the default route was not enabled, meaning that manual or customer-specific enhancements were required.

With this innovation, the invoicing carrier and invoicing carrier level can now be defined for each stage in the default route and are automatically transferred to the corresponding stage fields of the rail freight order.

This enables more practical, master-data-based modeling of rail freight orders involving complex transportation networks with multiple carriers and invoicing carriers, and significantly reduces the need for manual work or customer-specific enhancements.


Handover of Invoicing Carrier and Stage Invoicing Level to the Rail freight order

 

Clean Core: New OData V4 Web APIs in SAP S/4HANA

Feature Package 2, significant enhancements have been introduced to support a Clean Core strategy in Transportation Management through new OData V4 Web APIs. These APIs provide standardized, extensible, and upgrade-safe integration capabilities for key transportation business objects, enabling customers and partners to build modern integrations while keeping custom developments outside the SAP core.

The new APIs cover Freight Orders, Consignment Orders, Freight Bookings, Freight Units., Locations, and Organizational Units.  They support essential business operations such as creating, updating, retrieving, and canceling transportation documents, assigning and unassigning freight units and consignment orders, as well as reporting and revoking execution events. The APIs are designed to provide behavior that is consistent with the SAP Fiori applications wherever possible while also taking advantage of API-specific capabilities such as partial processing for mass operations.

A key focus of the development is extensibility. Customers can enhance the underlying Virtual Data Model (VDM) using key user extensibility and custom fields, allowing the APIs to adapt to individual business requirements without compromising the Clean Core approach. The APIs are released with C2 contracts, providing a stable foundation for customer and partner developments.

Together with other APIs, end-to-end business scenarios can be modelled that encompass, for example, sales orders or outbound deliveries, freight units, consignment orders, and freight orders through the interaction of these new APIs.

 New OData V4 Web APIs in SAP S/4HANA

Using the SAP's Process Test Framework developers can efficiently test and automate business processes while ensuring the same validation and business logic as the SAP user interface.
Documentation for the new APIs is available in the SAP Help Portal, with publication in the SAP Business Accelerator Hub underway.

Looking ahead, we plan to further expand these capabilities in Feature Package 3 with local APIs and business events, continuing to strengthen the Clean Core integration strategy for Transportation Management. 

 

These were the main innovations in TM for FP02.
If you are curious about what will be delivered with FP03, check the items published on the Roadmap Explorer..
You can also have a first grasp on the vision for innovations we plan to deliver with SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition 2027 and SAP S/4HANA 2027 OP and beyond.

Additionally enablement sessions for TM and the features delivered with FP02 are scheduled.
Please register with the following link to the sessions: Supply Chain Management webinars.

  • What’s New Viewer
  • SAP TM Product Page on sap.com
  • SAP Community for Transportation Management
  • SAP Transportation Management Group on LinkedIn

entry.title: How Joule Assistants Orchestrate: From User Intent to Coordinated Actions
entry.content:
Understanding how Joule Assistants orchestrate

I've had a lot of customer meetings lately where I'm asked to explain something I genuinely believe is one of the most impressive things SAP has built in AI: how Joule Assistants actually orchestrate work behind the scenes. With more meetings coming up and the same question certain to land again, I wasn't happy with the answer I'd been giving. I needed an easier way to explain it.

One night, I booked a restaurant for my wife and me. My wife has some dietary constraints due to allergies, so when the waiter arrived, she ordered the tasting menu but told him "no shellfish, no gluten, and no lactose." The waiter went to the kitchen, and while we were waiting, I found myself looking through the pass window. And something about the way the head chef was operating and directing the kitchen made me immediately see the analogy I'd been looking for.

In the kitchen, the head chef received our order, and I could see him reading and reasoning about it. He was understanding the request, breaking it down into tasks, and triggering, coordinating, and calling out tailored instructions to each station — accounting for every dietary constraint, adapting every course. "Course one, swap the crab for avocado, check the dressing is gluten-free, clean your board first." "Course three, seabass instead of scallop, olive oil only, no lactose on that pan." "Pastry — scrap the tart shell, do the berry sorbet, double-check it's gluten-free."

Each kitchen station got their specific instructions and nothing else. Some were working in parallel. Others were waiting for a prior step to complete. They didn't need to know what the other stations were doing. They just executed their piece and reported back.

Meanwhile, we were sitting at the table, having simply ordered dinner and waiting for it to arrive. What was happening in the kitchen was something we didn't need to think about. That's exactly how Joule Assistants work.

By the time dessert arrived, I had the whole thing mapped out. Let me walk you through it, because once you see the parallel, it's hard to unsee.

When a supply chain planner, a product engineer, or a maintenance supervisor type a request in Joule, that request moves through four distinct layers before anything happens in a SAP system. Each layer has a specific job, and each one maps neatly to someone in that restaurant.

Figure 1: The four layers between a user request and a system action

The first layer is the Joule Orchestrator. In the restaurant story, it would be the waiter. It reads your request, classifies the intent, checks the catalog of registered capabilities, enforces your access permissions, and routes to the best-matched Assistant. It doesn't cook anything. It just makes sure your order gets to the right kitchen and the right head chef.

The second layer is the Domain Assistant; in our story, it would be the head chef. This is where the real orchestration happens. The Assistant doesn't follow a predefined script. It plans and reasons by leveraging an LLM, the same way a skilled manager would think through a complex problem. It reads the request, identifies what's actually being asked, figures out which specialists can help, decides the order of operations, dispatches them, evaluates what they return, and synthesizes everything into a recommendation. That's a lot of invisible work happening before you see a single result.

The third layer is the Domain Agents; the kitchen stations. Each one is a specialist. They have a narrow, well-defined scope: one might be focused on demand trend analysis, another on inventory allocation modelling, a third on network capacity. They don't decide the broader workflow. They execute their piece, access the relevant SAP systems, and report back to the Assistant with structured findings.

The part that keeps coming back to me is the reasoning loop. Every request triggers a process inside the Domain Assistant. Understanding this is what separates a surface-level explanation from a real one.

Figure 2: The five-step reasoning loop every Domain Assistant runs

Step one is understanding the job. Not just reading the words, but working out the domain, the scope, the constraints, and what "done" actually looks like.

Step two is assembling the team. The Assistant selects which Agents to involve and deliberately excludes the ones that aren't relevant.

Step three is sequencing and dispatching tasks. If the tasks are independent of each other, the Assistant fans them out in parallel to save time. If they depend on each other — like a root cause analysis that must precede a resolution plan — they run in sequence, each one building on the last.

Step four is adaptive replanning. This is what separates orchestration from automation. Take a manufacturing quality use case example: the Manufacturing Assistant might initially plan to run an inspection readiness agent. But when the diagnostic agent comes back and reports that the root cause is contaminated supplier material — and not an equipment issue — the Assistant drops the inspection agent and adds a supplier nonconformance agent instead, mid-task. A rigid workflow would have run the wrong agents. The Assistant evaluated the evidence and changed course.

Step five is synthesis and governance. The Assistant combines all findings into a coherent recommendation and then decides about execution: sometimes the right answer is just showing you the insight, and sometimes it executes a direct action in a system.

Now we’re able to understand how a Joule Assistant orchestrates, but one piece is still missing: how do Assistants and Agents talk to each other? Every agent could be built by a different team, running on a different platform, in a different part of the enterprise. Without a shared protocol, connecting them would require building a custom bridge for every pair. This is exactly the problem the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol was designed to solve.

Figure 3: The three phases of A2A communication between Assistants and Agents

The protocol works in three steps. The Assistant first discovers an Agent by reading its "digital business card" — a structured document that describes what the Agent can do, what inputs it expects, how to reach it, and what outputs it can deliver. Then it delegates by sending a formal task object that includes the intent, parameters, constraints, and a channel for real-time updates. Then the Agent executes and collaborates, streaming progress back as it works, not just returning a result at the end.

Alongside A2A, agents use MCP (Model Context Protocol) to connect to APIs, planning models, data products, knowledge graphs, and third-party services. If A2A is how agents talk to each other, MCP is how agents access the tools they need to do the work.

One additional thing to understand is that a Joule Assistant and a Joule Agent are built from the same technology. Both are developed in Joule Studio. Both use LLMs for planning and reasoning. Both run on SAP Business AI Platform. Both are registered in the SAP AI Agent Hub. Both use the A2A and MCP protocols. Technically, they are the same construct, however, what differentiates them is a design decision. An Assistant is built with a broad, role-aware scope and the authority to coordinate others. An Agent is built with a narrow, task-specific scope and the authority to execute within it. Same kitchen, but different job descriptions.

When a planner, engineer, or supervisor makes a request in Joule, they express their intent once. The Joule Orchestrator routes it. The Assistant reasons through it and delegates the tasks. The Agents execute. The systems get updated. The human gets a recommendation and approves the action. Users never needed to know which agents were involved, in what order, or which systems were touched. They simply got an answer.

entry.title: Is Your Supply Chain Still Waiting for Things to Calm Down? I wouldn't hold your breath!
entry.content:
In the past weeks, Toyota and Honda halted production in Thailand because of monsoon floods. Stellantis shut plants in France and Italy over weak demand. The Iran war pushed diesel prices to record highs. And ocean container schedules became, in Sea-Intelligence's own words, "highly volatile placeholders." Not one crisis. Four. Simultaneously. On four different continents.

So here is the question your leadership team needs to answer honestly: are you still treating disruption as the exception, or have you started building a supply chain that performs in the here and now?

When "Disruption" Stops Being the Right Word

Language shapes strategy. And the word "disruption" has been quietly misleading us for years.

Disruption implies a departure from a stable baseline — a storm that passes, a shock that absorbs, a crisis with a clear end date. But Logistics Management's 37th Annual State of Logistics Report, published in October 2026, draws a starker conclusion:

 "Continuous disruption, from shifting trade policies and geopolitical tensions to labor shortages and rising costs, has become a         permanent feature of the global supply chain."

Not a phase. Not a recovery window. A permanent feature.

That reframes everything. If disruption is the operating environment, then every supply chain strategy still designed around the assumption of eventual calm is already obsolete. Capgemini's A World in Balance 2026: The Resilience Reset, which surveyed 2,100 senior executives across 70 countries, puts it bluntly:

 “Climate disruption, resource constraints, and geopolitical volatility have made resilience transformation a survival     requirement.”

Not a competitive advantage. A survival requirement.

The Convergence Problem: It's Not One Thing, It's Everything at Once

Here is what makes the current operating environment fundamentally different from past cycles of volatility: it's not a single spike. It's a collision.

Netstock research from September 2026 found that the defining supply chain challenge of 2026 is no longer solving an individual disruption. It's managing multiple simultaneous pressures:

  • Supplier lead-time swings (cited by 29% of respondents)
  • Raw material costs (23%)
  • Freight rate volatility
  • Unpredictable demand shifts
  • Deteriorating inventory performance

All converging at the same time!

Traditional supply chain planning was designed for sequences: one issue resolves, another appears, you adapt.

Today's environment doesn't offer that luxury. You're managing floods in Asia-Pacific, energy shocks in Europe, and sourcing constraints in North America simultaneously, with ripple effects that intersect in ways your planning models were never designed to predict.

The executives who are winning aren't smarter. They have better visibility across the whole picture, faster.

Designing for Constant Motion, Not Occasional Calm

If disruption is permanent, the architecture of resilience has to change. You cannot bolt agility onto a supply chain designed for efficiency. You have to design for motion from the start.

The DP World CSCO Pulse Report from August 2026 a clear signal of where leadership thinking is already moving:

  • Eighty-four percent of CSCOs say they have shifted their primary strategy from cost reduction to resilience and optionality.
  • Seventy-one percent plan to diversify their supplier base within the next 12 months.
  • 93% say their role in driving business growth has become more central over the past three years.

That last number matters. Supply chain is no longer a back-office function absorbing shocks for the rest of the business. It is the business! And supply chain leaders know it.

Manufacturers are also beginning to map their supplier ecosystems through a new lens, not just cost and lead time, but resilience risk:

    Which single-source supplier could bring your production to a halt tomorrow?

    Which tier-two relationship hides a geopolitical concentration you've never modelled?

Real-time visibility into these dependencies isn't a reporting feature. It's a survival capability.

The Executive Shift: From Recovery to Readiness

There is a useful way to divide supply chain organisations right now: those still optimising for the last disruption, and those designing for the next one.

Recovery thinking looks like this: identify what broke, fix it, restore baseline. It's reactive by nature. It treats every crisis as a temporary deviation rather than a data point about the new operating reality.

Readiness thinking looks different. It builds sensing capabilities that flag stress before it becomes failure. It maintains strategic optionality (alternative suppliers, flexible routing, distributed inventory) not because those options are cheap, but because the cost of not having them is catastrophic. It treats agility not as a crisis response but as a standard operating mode.

 

How prepared is your organization to sense, decide, and move faster than the disruption?

The supply chains that will define the next decade aren't the ones built for efficiency in stable times. They're the ones built for performance in unstable ones. The executives leading those organisations have stopped asking when things will settle down,  and started asking what their supply chain can do right now, under pressure, at speed.

Disruption isn't the interruption. It's the job.

The question isn't whether disruption is coming. It's whether your supply chain is designed to keep moving when it does.

entry.title: How the Supply Chain Planning Assistant Orchestrates an Inventory Decision
entry.content:
A demand spike, one question, and how Joule orchestrates the answer

Previously I wrote about how Joule Assistants orchestrate work behind the scenes, and I used a restaurant kitchen to explain it (here that post). The analogy did its job to explain how Joule Assistants orchestrate, but nothing better than showing it with a real world scenario. 

So this time, no analogy. Let me walk you through a real supply chain planning moment, exactly as it unfolds, and show you everything Joule does between a planner’s request and the answer that lands on their screen.

Picture a supply chain planner, in this case I'll call her Elena. She is responsible for inventory across EMEA. It’s early Q4, and the numbers in front of her don’t match the plan since the demand is spiking, and the usual year-end pressure is building up. She needs to protect service levels without blowing through her working capital target.

She has one question that matters more than anything else on her screen:

“I see a demand spike in Q4 for EMEA. Where should I invest inventory to maximize fill rate without exceeding my working capital target?”

One or more years ago, answering that would honestly have meant days of work: pulling demand signals, running allocation scenarios, checking which distribution centers could physically absorb more stock, and reconciling all of it against a capital ceiling, usually across three different teams and a dozen spreadsheets.

Elena types it into Joule instead. A few moments later, she has a specific, defensible recommendation: which SKUs, how much, which locations, and how it fits her budget. Here’s everything that happened in between:

When Elena hits enter, her request moves through four distinct layers before anything happens in a SAP system.

Figure 1: The four layers between a planner’s question and a system action

The first layer is the Joule Orchestrator. It reads her request, classifies the intent — supply chain planning, inventory optimization — confirms she’s authenticated and holds the right IBP access, and routes her to the best-matched Assistant, in this case the Supply Chain Planning Assistant. The Joule Orchestrator doesn’t do the planning itself. It just makes sure her question reaches the right expert.

The second layer is the Supply Chain Planning Assistant. This is where the orchestration happens. It doesn’t follow a predefined script — it reasons, leveraging an LLM, the way an experienced planning manager would think through a hard problem. It reads the request, works out what’s actually being asked, decides which specialists can help, dispatches them, evaluates what they return, and synthesizes everything into a recommendation.

The third layer is the specialist Agents. Each one is a narrow expert — one for demand trends, one for inventory investment allocation, one for the distribution footprint. They don’t own the broader decision. They answer their piece, pull from the relevant systems, and report back to the Assistant with structured findings.

The part I find most interesting is what the Supply Chain Planning Assistant does in its “head”, and here it is, filled in with Elena’s actual question.

Figure 2: The five-step reasoning loop every Domain Assistant runs

Step one is understanding the job. The Assistant frames the problem: the domain is inventory planning, the scope is Q4 and EMEA, the hard constraint is the working capital target, and the expected outcome is a specific recommendation — where to invest, how much, and which SKUs. Not a dashboard, but rather a decision.

Step two is assembling the team. The Assistant selects three agents: a Demand Trend Agent, an Inventory Investment Allocation Agent, and a Footprint Optimization Agent. These agents are deliberately chosen because they address the specific scope, need, constraints, and expected outcome based on the user request. Just as importantly, it excludes the ones that don’t fit the request. The request isn’t about explaining an existing plan or ranking orders; it’s about where to put inventory. Choosing the right team is half the job.

Step three is sequencing and dispatching. The Assistant recognizes these three questions are independent of each other - understanding the demand spike doesn’t depend on knowing warehouse capacity - so instead of running them one after another, it dispatches all three out in parallel. Three specialists working simultaneously, which is why Elena gets her answer in moments, not hours.

Step four is monitoring and replanning. As the agents report back, the Assistant checks whether the findings change the picture. The Footprint Agent flags that the distribution center in Milan is constrained while the Frankfurt and Rotterdam distribution centers have room. Does that force a rethink? No, it actually confirms Frankfurt and Rotterdam as the right homes for the extra stock, so no replanning is needed. (When the evidence does change the picture, this is exactly where the Assistant adapts; swapping agents mid-task, as I described in the last post.)

Step five is synthesis and governance. The Assistant pulls the three findings into one coherent recommendation: increase safety stock for SKUs A, B and C at Frankfurt and Rotterdam; hold SKU D, which isn’t worth the capital; total investment €2.1M, comfortably inside the €2.5M target. Then it makes a governance decision. Acting on this means pushing new targets to SAP IBP and updating MRP in S/4HANA — a change that touches multiple systems and needs an audit trail. So rather than firing off changes directly, the Assistant presents the recommendation to Elena for review and, on her approval, triggers a governed multi-system workflow.

What makes the recommendation trustworthy is that every line of it traces back to a specialist’s finding. Elena sees the evidence, not just the conclusion.

Figure 3: The three specialist agents and what each returned

The Demand Trend Agent confirms the spike is seasonal plus promotional, +35% above baseline, and that it normalizes in Q1, so this is a short-term investment, not a structural shift. The Inventory Investment Allocation Agent finds that SKUs A, B and C deliver the fill-rate improvement for €2.1M, while SKU D doesn’t justify the capital. The Footprint Optimization Agent confirms Frankfurt, at 72% utilization, and Rotterdam, at 68%, can absorb the additional stock, while Milan, at 94%, cannot. Three narrow experts, three focused answers, assembled into one decision.

A question I always get: how do these assistants and agents work together, especially when they might be built by different teams? The answer is a shared protocol. SAP has adopted the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol (an open standard) so the Supply Chain Planning Assistant can discover an agent by reading its “digital business card”, delegate a structured task to it, and collaborate as the agent streams its results back. Alongside A2A, agents use MCP (Model Context Protocol) to reach the tools and data they need such as SAP IBP, S/4HANA, planning models, data products, APIs. If A2A is how agents talk to each other, MCP is how they reach the systems and tools they need.

At the end, Elena asked one question. She never had to know how the Joule Orchestrator classified her intent, nor that the Supply Chain Planning Assistant assembled a team of three specialists, nor that they ran against IBP and S/4HANA, or that the whole thing was reconciled against her capital target before it reached her. She just got an answer she could act on and the authority to approve it.

That’s the whole idea. The orchestration happens behind the scenes, and the planner is left with the one thing they actually needed: a n optimal, clear, auditable, and defensible decision. That is how Joule Assistants orchestrate - not in a kitchen this time, but in the middle of a real Q4.

entry.title: SAP PP/DS: Understanding Firming in Production Planning
entry.content:
1. Introduction

In SAP Production Planning and Detailed Scheduling (PP/DS), firming is used to protect selected planning elements from automatic changes during planning runs.

During production planning, the system may reschedule or modify planned orders to respond to changing demand, material availability, and capacity constraints. Firming helps the planner retain control over selected planning decisions.

2. What Is Firming?

Firming is a mechanism that restricts changes to planning elements during planning activities, depending on the applicable firming settings and planning process.

It is particularly important when planners want to preserve an agreed production plan while allowing the system to continue planning other orders and requirements.

3. Why Is Firming Required?

Firming helps to:

1. Protect selected planned orders from unwanted changes.

2. Stabilize the production schedule after planning decisions have been made.

3. Support coordination between material availability, production capacity, and delivery commitments.

4. Reduce unnecessary rescheduling of orders that are already agreed upon or prepared for execution.

5. How Does Firming Work in SAP PP/DS?

The system determines how planning elements are treated based on their firming status and the relevant planning settings.

For example, a planned order may be firmed after the planner has reviewed its production dates and confirmed material availability.

During subsequent planning runs, the firming settings influence whether the system can change the order or its scheduling details.

The exact behavior depends on the planning element, firming mechanism, planning procedure, and configuration.

5. Firming and the Planning Time Fence

The planning time fence is an important concept in production planning.

It defines a period within which planning changes are restricted according to the applicable settings. Firming, however, is not the same as the planning time fence.

A planning time fence controls planning behavior within a defined time horizon, whereas firming can protect specific planning elements according to the relevant firming rules.

6. Practical Business Scenario

Consider a manufacturing company producing industrial pumps.

The planner creates planned orders for the next two weeks. After reviewing component availability, machine capacity, and customer delivery dates, the planner decides to firm selected orders.

When a subsequent planning run is executed, the firming settings help protect those selected orders while the system continues to plan other requirements.

This supports a more controlled and stable production planning process.
